Al-nashat is also used for the movement of a wild bull and of a camel, because of the strength of that; so the noun described is either the wandering stars, as a figure of speech for the constancy of their movement in their orbits, or the camels of the raid, or the angels who hasten to execute what God commanded of the affair of creation; and both are in a literal sense. In any case, its conjunction with al-nazi'at is conjunction of one kind upon another kind or of one category upon another category.

And (nashtan) is a verbal noun that came in the form of the verbal noun of the transitive fa'ala of the pattern nasara, so it is determined that (al-nashitat) are doers of nashat, so it is transitive.

It may be that it is inherently transitive, intended for the real activity and not the metaphorical. It is also possible that the emphasis is to establish the attribute and not to remove the possibility of metaphor.

From Ibn 'Abbas: al-nashitat are the angels who energize the souls of the believers; and from him: they are the souls of the believers that become active for departure.

And (al-sabihat) is an attribute from metaphorical sabh; the root of sabh is swimming, which is the movement of the body directly upon the surface of water, and here it is borrowed for swiftness of movement. So it is possible that the intended are the angels travelling in the atmospheres of the heavens and the horizons of the earth; this was narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

It is also possible that the intended are the horses of the warriors when they swiftly attack the enemy, like the swimmer in water, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays describing a horse:

"Sleek, when the swimming ones upon the battlefield raised the dust with the trodden dry earth."

It was also said: (al-sabihat) are the stars, which accords with the view of those who explained al-nazi'at as the stars. (Sabhan) is an emphatic verbal noun for the purpose of confirming the reality, through the means to an exalting emphasis. The conjunction of (fa-al-sabiqat) with fa' indicates that this attribute branches off from the one before it, because they conjoin with fa' the attributes which by nature some of them branch from others, as already mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By those who set in ranks, in rows﴾ [al-Saffat: 1], ﴿then those who drive away with a driving﴾ [al-Saffat: 2], ﴿then those who recite the reminder﴾ [al-Saffat: 3], and the saying of Ibn Zayyabah:

"Alas for Zayyabah for al-Harith al-Sabih, then al-Ghanim, then al-Ayib."

Therefore (fa-al-sabiqat) are the ones among the swimmers that are foremost.

Al-sabq: the passing of a traveller over one who travels with him and his arrival at the place travelled to before him. Sabq is also used for swiftness of arrival without anyone travelling with the one who is ahead; He, exalted, said: ﴿So race to the good things﴾ and He said: ﴿Those are they who hasten toward good deeds, and they are foremost in them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60].

Sabq is also used for overcoming and subjugation, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 21], and the saying of Murrah ibn 'Adda' al-Faq'asi:

"As if you had not been outrun by time for a single night, when you reached what you were seeking."

So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then those who race ahead, a racing﴾ is suitable to be carried upon these meanings, according to the different senses of the description of (al-sabihat), each as fits its own probability: that they be the ones travelling swiftly in what you know, or those who hasten. And if (al-sabihat) means horses, then (al-sabiqat), if understood as meaning those who advance quickly, is a metonymy for the riders' indifference to their enemy and their eagerness to reach the enemy's land; or in the sense of their overcoming their enemies.

It is emphasised with the verbal noun synonymous with its meaning, which is (sabqan), for emphasis, and because the indefiniteness indicates the greatness of that racing.

Al-mudabbirat: those described by management (al-tadbir).

Al-tadbir: the roaming of thought over the consequences of things, and the carrying out of affairs in a manner suitable to that for which they exist. If al-sabihat are groups of angels, then the meaning of their management is the execution of what has been entrusted to them in the most perfect manner in which they were permitted, and this is expressed by management of affairs because it resembles the action of a steadfast manager.

If al-sabihat are the horses of the warriors, then the intended tadbir is the management of the stratagems of war: charging, retreating, raiding, killing, capturing, pursuing the fleeing, or holding ground. Attributing management to the horses on this view is a rational metaphor, because the management belongs to the riders, and the horses are merely means for executing the management, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep mountain pass﴾ [al-Hajj: 27]. So the coming is attributed to the pronoun of "every lean camel" [al-Hajj: 27], because the coming of the pilgrims from deep mountain passes takes place by the travel of camels.

In this metaphor there is an allusion to the skill of the horses and the swiftness with which they understand the intentions of their riders, to the point that they seem to be the ones managing what their riders had managed.

Al-amr: the matter and the important purpose; its tanwin is for glorification, and its singular form is for intending the genus, i.e., affairs.

From the totality of the attributes (al-nazi'at, al-nashitat, al-sabihat), if they are understood as groups of archers, camel-drivers and horsemen, it may be that it is an indication to the kinds of combatants: infantry, namely the archers with bows, and cavalry on horses; and the archers used to walk in front of the cavalry, shielding them with arrows until they reached the place of battle. Unays ibn Zabban al-Ta'i said:

"And beneath the chests of the horses is a rough-skinned, firm-footed one, whose arrows are dispensed to the hearts that are heedless."

And because the verse bears these possibilities, it was an allusion threatening the polytheists with a war to be launched against them, namely the raid of the conquest of Makkah or the raid of Badr, like the surah of (al-'Adiyat) and its kind; and it is one of the proofs of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), since these threats, explicit and allusive, occurred during his stay in Makkah while the Muslims were weak; thus there resulted from this oath an allusion to a punishment in this world.

The clause from ﴿on the Day when the Quaking will quake﴾ to (khashi'ah) is the answer to the oath, and the explicit speech is an admonition. The intended meaning of it is its necessary implication, which is the occurrence of the Resurrection, since hearts exist only in bodies. It is known that the intended meaning of ﴿on the Day when the Quaking will quake﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, since it has been defined by such states in many verses revealed earlier, such as His saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4]. So in this answer there is an amplification of the Day of Resurrection, and within it a confirmation of its occurrence; thus there results a brevity in speech combining a warning of its occurrence and a caution against what takes place in it.

Surah 79, verses 1–9 (part 2 of 2)

And ﴿On the Day the Quaking One quakes﴾ is an adverbial complement related to (wājifah) (trembling). This leads to the conclusion that the thing sworn to, whose realization is intended, is the occurrence of resurrection (al-ba'th), expressed in a style that makes a stronger impression on the hearers who deny it than a direct statement of the answer to the oath would. For some of its circumstances, which are among its terrors, indicate what is sworn to, so the answer to the oath carries a warning.

The answer clause was not joined with the oath particle of response (lam al-jawab) because of the distance between the answer and the oath, owing to the length of the oath clause. It appears to me from the usage of eloquent speakers that when the distance between the oath and the answer is great, they do not bring the lam of oath into the answer. Among examples of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the sky containing the constellations﴾ [al-Buruj: 1] up to ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾ [al-Buruj: 4]. Its like is abundant in the Qur'an. So the lam of oath is not brought into its answer except when the answer immediately follows the oath clause, such as ﴿And by God, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiya': 57] and ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92]. Also, because when the answer to an oath is a nominal clause, its being joined with the lam of response is not common. I have not seen an explicit statement permitting or prohibiting this, although the author of al-Mughni (Ibn Hisham) inclined in the discussion of the lam of response, regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they had believed and feared God, a reward from God would have been better﴾ [al-Baqarah: 103], that the lam is the lam of response to a deleted oath and not the lam of the answer to (law) (if), on the evidence that the clause is nominal, and nominal clauses are rare as answers to (law). Thus he did not regard a nominal answer clause as joined with the lam. The author of al-Kashshaf, following al-Farra' and others, considered the answer to the oath to be deleted, its estimated form being: "You will surely be resurrected" (latub'athunna).

The adverbial complement was placed before its governing element because that adverbial is the most important element in the answer to the oath, since what is intended is the affirmation of its occurrence. Placing the adverbial first serves to give it emphasis and attention. When the speech is emphasized by the oath, the emphasis extends to the complements of the statement, among which is that adverbial, and emphasis is a form of attention. Then that adverbial was further emphasized in the middle of the speech by His saying: (yawma'idhin) (on that day), which is (﴿On the Day the Quaking One quakes﴾). Thus a great concern is achieved for this statement.

Page 67

And al-rajf (rajf) is agitation and shaking, and its verb is of the pattern (naṣara). The apparent meaning of the words of the lexicographers is that it is an intransitive verb, and I have not seen anyone say that it is used transitively. Therefore it is permissible for the attribution of (tarjuf) (quakes) to (al-rājifah) (the quaking one) to be literal. Then what is meant by (al-rājifah) is the earth, because it trembles and shakes with the earthquakes that occur at the end of the worldly realm and the passage to the otherworldly realm. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day the earth and the mountains quake﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14], and He said: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a shaking﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4]. The feminine form of (al-rājifah) is because it is the earth. In that case, the meaning of ﴿Followed by the following one﴾ is that another quaking follows the previous quaking, because the description of the quaking one requires the occurrence of a quaking, so the following one is a second quaking that follows the first.

It is also permissible for the attribution of (tarjuf) to (al-rājifah) to be a metonymic attribution (majaz 'aqli), where the quaking one is used for the cause of the quaking.

Then what is meant by (al-rājifah) is the blast and the earthquake by which the earth quakes; it has been made to be the quaking one by way of hyperbole, like their saying: "a pleasing life" (ʿīshah rāḍiyah). This is the one that suits His saying: ﴿Followed by the following one﴾, that is, it follows that quaking one; that is, the cause of the quaking is followed by a following one, that is, one that occurs after it.

It is also permissible for al-rajf to be used metaphorically for the intensity of a sound, so an intense sound is likened to al-rajf, which is violent shaking.

The feminine form of (al-rājifah) on this reading is for interpreting it as an event or occurrence.

And ﴿followed by the following one﴾: the one that comes after. It is said: radifa, meaning tabi'a (followed). Al-radif is that which follows another. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿that I will reinforce you with three thousand angels following one another﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 124], that is, a second one follows the first quaking. So what is meant is a following one of the same kind, and they are the two blasts mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious, except whom God wills. Then it will be blown again, and at once they will be standing, looking on﴾ [al-Zumar: 68].

The clause ﴿followed by the following one﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to al-rājifah.

The indefinite form of (qulūb) (hearts) is for multiplicity, that is, many hearts; for this reason it occurred as a subject while being indefinite, to intend the category.

Page 68

What is meant is the hearts of the polytheists who used to deny resurrection, for when they rise and know that what the Messenger ﷺ promised them is true, they anticipate what he had warned them of: the punishment for denying resurrection, polytheism, and other such conditions of theirs.

As for the hearts of the believers, there is in them a tranquility that varies according to their varying degrees of piety.

Fear on that day, although no one is free of it, is most intense among those who are certain of an evil end and know that they were astray in the worldly life.

Al-wājifah: the one that is agitated by fear. It is said: wajafa (like daraba) wajfan, wajīfan, wujūfan, when it becomes agitated.

(wājifah) is the predicate of (qulūb).

The clause ﴿their eyes are humbled﴾ is a second predicate regarding (qulūb), and His saying ﴿their eyes are humbled﴾ has added clarification to the meaning of the agitation, that is, the eyes of the owners of the hearts.

Khushu' (humility) is in its real sense submission and abasement, and it is a state of a person. Attributing it to eyes is a metaphor for lowering and glancing with a furtive glance from intense dread and fear of the dreadful things they witness of evil treatment. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿their eyes humbled﴾ [al-Qamar: 7] in the surah (﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar: 1]). Its like is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 24].

The attribution of (abṣār) (eyes) to the pronoun of (qulūb) (hearts) is due to the slightest connection, since the eyes belong to the owners of the hearts, and both are limbs of the bodies, like His saying: ﴿except for an evening or its morning﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 46].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 79, verses 10–11:

﴿They say, "Are we indeed to be returned to our former state?"﴾ ﴿"Even when we have become decayed bones?"﴾

This is a resumptive clause (istinaf). It may be an initial resumption (istinaf ibtida'i), following the oath and its response, to indicate that these are the people who will be among those whose hearts tremble and whose eyes are downcast on the day when the Quaking (al-Rajifa) shakes.

It may also be an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because the oath and what follows of threat raise a question in the mind of the listener about who is behind this oath. It is answered by ﴿They say, "Are we indeed to be returned to our former state?"﴾, meaning: they deny the Resurrection. For this reason the speech about their saying is given in the third person (ghayba), as is the case when speaking of someone who is not present.

The pronoun in (yaqulun) refers to something known from the context: they are the people who are notorious for this statement, and they are not hidden to one who knows their conditions and their discourse. They are the polytheists in their denial of the Resurrection.

The speech is addressed to everyone who can hear it among the Muslims and others.

It is also permissible that the speech is addressed to those who deny the Resurrection, by way of indirect address (iltifat).

Their statement is related in the present tense (mudari') to indicate that they persist in it, that it is continually renewed among them, and that they do not desist from it.

The present tense also evokes the state in which they are, by repeating this saying, so that this becomes a metaphor (kinaya) for amazement at their statement, like the saying of God, Exalted: ﴿When fear had left Abraham and the good news had come to him, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74].

The listener knows that they did not repeat this saying except that they had said it in the past.

This statement issues from them while they are in this world, so the pronoun in (yaqulun) does not refer to (qulub) in the words of God, Exalted: ﴿Hearts on that day will be trembling﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 8].

It was their custom to express the speech in which they deny the Resurrection in the form of a question, presenting themselves in the appearance of one who is hesitant and inquiring, for the purpose of mockery and of wonder at the matter being asked about. The intended meaning is denial, since they claim that the argument for the impossibility of the Resurrection is valid.

The amazed question (al-istifham al-ta'ajjubi) is placed before a nominal sentence confirmed by (inna), by the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), and these are three emphasizers strengthening the predicate, to indicate that they utter what expresses amazement at the report, and at the extreme certainty of the Muslims concerning it. So they wonder at accepting this report, let alone at verifying it and being certain of it.

The (mardud) is the thing returned to its owner after it has been benefited from, like a loan (ariyya), or the return of the price of a sold item when a contract is annulled (tafasukh) or cancelled by mutual agreement (taqayul). That is: "Are we indeed to be returned (lamurja'una) to life?" That is: "Are we indeed to be resurrected from our graves?"

[Page 70]

What is meant by (al-hafira) is the former state, that is, life.

The uses of (al-hafira) are numerous in the speech of the Arabs, and the literal meaning cannot be distinguished from the figurative among them. The most evident explanation is that of al-Kashshaf: it is said, "So-and-so returned to his hafira," that is, on his path by which he came, in which he left an impression (hafara) by walking in it. The traces of his two feet are described as a hafr (a groove), because his two feet were placed in it, forming a trace like a hafr. He also indicated that describing the path as hafira means "possessing a hafr." It is also permitted that it is a rational metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli), like their saying "a pleasing life" (ʿisha radiya), meaning "one whose life is pleasing to its liver." They also say, "He returned to the hafira," as an image for one who was in a state, then left it, then returned to it, so that it became, "he returned in the hafira" and "he was restored to the hafira," functioning as a proverb.

From this is the verse of the poet, who is 'Imran ibn Hittan, as Ibn al-Sayyid al-Batalyusi supposed in his commentary on Adab al-Kuttab:

Hafira, upon baldness and grey hair? God forbid, from folly and shame!

Among the proverbs is their saying: "The payment is at the hafira," that is, giving the prize of the race to the winner upon his arrival at the appointed goal of the race.

He means: "Is it a return to the hafira?"

The adverbial clause of time (zarf) (idha) in His words, (﴿when we have become decayed bones﴾), is the locus of the amazement and the claim of impossibility, that is: "when we have become decayed, rotten bones, how then will we return alive?"

(Idha) is related to (mardudun).

(Nakhira) is a descriptive adjective derived from their saying: "the bone decayed" (nakhira al-'azm), when it rotted and became hollow in the middle like a reed. The feminine form of (nakhira) is because its described noun is a broken plural (jam' taksir), and its description is used in the feminine in usage.

The hamza of (idha) is a hamza of interrogation. Ibn Kathir? [no]

It is the hamza of (idha). The rest of the Ten Readers (al-'ashara) read (a-idha) with two hamzas: one of them is an open hamza of interrogation, and the second is a kasra hamza, which is the hamza of (idha).

This interrogation is a denying interrogation, emphasizing the first interrogation, to indicate that this state is deserving of an increase in denial of return to life after death. So these are two denials to show the extreme impossibility of it.

[Page 71]

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (nakhiratan) without an alif after the nun. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Ruways from Ya'qub, and Khalaf read (nakhiratan) with an alif, as (nakira/nakhira variant readings: 'ākhira? — noted as read with alif).

Verse 12: ﴿They said, "That, then, would be a losing return."﴾

(They said) is a substitutive apposition (badal ishtimal) for the clause ﴿They say, "Will we indeed be returned to our former state?"﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 10].

The verb of saying is repeated for several purposes. One is to indicate that this statement of theirs was made with a different aim from the first statement. Their first statement was intended as denial and rejection, whereas the second was intended as mockery and derision (tawarruk), because they did not believe in that return. Their description of it as "losing" (khasirah) is therefore a matter of supposition and hypothesis, meaning: if a return were to occur, it would be a losing one. Another purpose is to prevent the assumption that the clause ﴿That, then, is a losing return﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) from the side of God Most High.

Their statement is expressed in the past tense rather than the present, unlike ﴿They say, "Will we indeed be returned to our former state?"﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 10], because this saying was uttered in mockery and so is not something repeated by them; whereas their words ﴿Will we indeed be returned to our former state?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 10] are, in their view, a compelling argument, so that is something they repeat in every situation. For this reason the purpose was not to express wonder at their statement, since wonder implies denial, while the fact that their return (karrah), that is, their coming back to life, would be a losing return is a established matter that cannot be denied, since they will certainly return to life as losers.

"That" (tilka) is a reference to the return (raddah) implied by "returned" (mardudun), and the use of the feminine demonstrative to refer to it is in order to predicate of it "return" (karrah).

"Then" (idhan) is a response to the preceding speech, the implied sense being: "then that is a losing return." "That" (tilka) has been placed before the particle of response for the sake of emphasis on the demonstrative.

Karrah is one instance of karr, which is returning after going away, that is, a return.

Khusran (loss) originally means the reduction of trading capital, which is meant to seek profit, that is, by an increase in wealth. It is here used figuratively for encountering something disliked and unexpected.

Describing the return as "losing" is a rational metonymy (majaz 'aqli) for emphasis, since the losers are its people. The meaning is: "Then we would indeed be losers, for having denied it and for the truth of the one who warned us of that return becoming evident."

The fa' here is *fasihah* (an eloquent fa', one that signals an unstated premise), and it marks a consequence drawn from their statement: ﴿Will we really be returned to our former state?﴾ [An-Nazi'at 79:10] ﴿When we are bones, decayed?﴾ [An-Nazi'at 79:11], from their deeming life after decay and annihilation impossible.

The sense of the passage is: "So there is no cause for wonder in that. It is only a single shout, and then, behold, you are present at the gathering."

The pronoun in *hiya* ("it") is *damir al-qissah*, the pronoun of the narrative or matter (also called *damir al-sha'n*, the pronoun of the situation). The feminine form was chosen so that it could properly refer back to *zajrah* ("shout"), and this is one of the finest uses of this pronoun. The restriction (*qasr*) expressed here is real (*haqiqi*), and its purpose is to emphasise the statement by treating the listener as one who believes that a single shout is not sufficient to bring them back to life.

The fa' in ﴿then, behold, they are in the *sahirah*﴾ is a consequence of the clause "it is only a single shout". The *idha* is *al-fuja'iyyah* (the *idha* of suddenness), meaning that the event occurs without delay. Thus the fa' and the sudden *idha* together reinforce the sense of consequence conveyed by the fa', which indicates that there is no interval between the shout and their presence in the *sahirah*.

The *zajrah* is a single instance of *zajr*, which is speech containing a command or prohibition uttered in a state of anger. It is said: "He *zajara* the camel," when he shouted at it to make it rise or move on. The word is used here metaphorically for God's command to bring the bodies of the dead into existence, depicting the command as one of compulsion, so that the coming into being is hastened. There is a correspondence with the revival of what was lifeless, just as a kneeling camel is roused by a shout, rising quickly out of fear of its driver. This is expressed elsewhere as the Cry in God's words: ﴿The day they hear the Cry in truth; that is the day of coming forth﴾ [Qaf 50:42], which is the same event described as the blowing of the Trumpet.

The *zajrah* is described as *wahidah* ("single") to reinforce what is already implied by the singular form of the noun, lest it be supposed that the singularity is merely a matter of the category (*nau'iyyah*). This shout is the second blast mentioned in God's words: [p. 73] ﴿And the Trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is in the earth swoons, except whom God wills. Then it is blown again, and behold, they stand looking on﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:68]. It is therefore the second of the two blasts, and it is the *radifah* (the following blast) mentioned earlier. That it is called "single" means that it is not followed by a second one. It is described as single in Surat al-Haqqah in this same sense.

The *sahirah* is level, white ground on which no vegetation grows, the kind of land chosen for the gathering of crowds and the placing of spoils. Here it means the land which God will make a place for the gathering of people for the Resurrection.

The use of the sudden *idha* indicates the speed with which they will be present in this place immediately following the resurrection. Its connection by the fa' serves to confirm the meaning that *idha* conveys, since combining suddenness with consequence is the strongest way of expressing speed while keeping the wording concise.

The meaning is that God, by the command of creation, orders the bodies to be created, into which the spirits that were in the world will enter, so that they are present at the place of gathering for reckoning, swiftly.

These verses form a digression (*i'tiraḍ*, an interjected passage) between the clause ﴿Then it will be but a single shout﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 13] and the clause ﴿Are you more difficult to create or is the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27], which is the proof for the establishment of the Resurrection, followed by a warning about what comes after it. The digression was called for by the fitting relevance of a threat to those who deny what the Messenger ﷺ told them about the Resurrection, because the condition of the polytheists in their rebellion against God and His Messenger ﷺ resembles the condition of Pharaoh and his people, and the condition of the Messenger ﷺ with his people resembles the condition of Moses (peace be upon him) with Pharaoh. The purpose is that the mention of the story of Moses should bring consolation to the Messenger ﷺ and admonition to the polytheists and their leaders, such as Abu Jahl, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and their likes, in accordance with His saying at its end: ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for those who fear﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26].

The interrogative ﴿Has there come to you﴾ (*hal atāka*) is a *ṣūrī* interrogative (an interrogative in form only), the purpose of which in such constructions is to arouse the listener's eagerness for the good news, without intending to ask the addressee whether he already knows that report. Thus it makes no difference whether he knew it before or not. For this reason the speaker does not wait for an answer from the one addressed; rather, he follows the interrogative with a detailed account of what the interrogative had left vague, as a way of indicating the importance of the report, to the point that it is something people ask about.

For this reason the Arabs do not use any interrogative particle in such a context other than *hal* (هل), because it indicates a request for the verification of the matter asked about. Thus in interrogation it is like *qad* (قد) in assertion, and the interrogative sense is present with it through the implied interrogative *hamza* (أ). The one who uses it asks about the confirmation of the matter. Of the same kind is their saying in questions: *alaysa qad ʿalimta kadhā* (ألَيْسَ قَدْ عَلِمْتَ كَذا, "Did you not know that such-and-such...?"), where they use *qad* with a negative verb accompanied by an interrogative of denial, without the addressee's knowledge being established in the speaker's mind.

The address is to an unspecified person. Thus the speech is an admonition, and it is followed by the consolation of the Messenger ﷺ.

The word ﴿atāka﴾ (أتاكَ) means "reached you." The verb "to come" (*ityān*) is used metaphorically for the acquisition of knowledge, likening the intelligible to the perceptible: it is as if the acquisition were a person arriving, in the explicit form of the metaphor (*tashbīhiyya*). Or it is as if the report that has arrived were a person to whom coming is ascribed, by way of the implicit metaphor (*istiʿāra makniyya*). Al-Nabigha said:

*"Your message reached me, may you not be cursed, that you had blamed me."*

The word ﴿al-ḥadīth﴾ (الحَدِيثُ) means "report." Its root form is *faʿīl* in the sense of *fāʿil*, from *ḥadatha al-amr* when a matter occurs and comes into being, i.e., "the occurring thing" among human affairs. It is applied to report only with an omitted *muḍāf* (a genitive noun understood), because of its frequent use. Its implied form is "the report of the occurrence," i.e., "the report of what occurred."

The word ﴿idh﴾ (إذا) is a noun of time, here used for the past. It is a *badal* (substitute) for ﴿ḥadīth Mūsā﴾ (the story of Moses), a *badal ishtimāl* (inclusive substitute), because the story of Moses includes God's speaking to him and other matters.

Just as ﴿idh﴾ may be a substitute for the object in His saying: ﴿And remember the favor of God upon you when you were enemies﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 103], it may also be a substitute for the subject and other things. The limiting of it by Ibn Hishām and others to being an object or a substitute for the object is a limitation to most of its uses when it is used outside the sense of a time adverb. It has been permitted in the *Kashshāf* (of al-Zamakhsharī) for ﴿idh﴾ to function as a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) in the reading of the one who recites: ﴿God has certainly conferred favor upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 164], in the Chapter of Āl ʿImrān.

[p. 74]

The word ﴿idh﴾ is attached to the clause ﴿his Lord called to him﴾ (*nādāhu rabbuhu*). The meaning is: "Has there come to you the report of a time when Moses called to his Lord?"

The word ﴿wādī﴾ (الوادِ) means a low place between mountains.

The word ﴿al-muqaddas﴾ (المُقَدَّسُ) means "purified." What is meant by it is a spiritual purification, which is honor and blessing because of what God's speech descended there, without an angel intermediating to convey the speech to Moses (peace be upon him). That is a special sanctification, and for this reason God said to him in the other verse: ﴿So remove your sandals; indeed, you are in the sacred valley﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 12].

The word ﴿Ṭuwā﴾ (طُوًى) is a place name. It is perhaps a kind of valley resembling a well that has been lined with stones (*maṭwiyya*). A place near Mecca has been named Dhū Ṭuwā, pronounced with *ḍamma*, *fatḥa*, and *kasra* on the *ṭāʾ*. This was mentioned in the Chapter of Ṭā-Hā. This is a valley on the side of Mount Sinai, in the desert of Sinai, on its western side.

The majority of readers (*al-Jumhūr*) recite *Ṭuwā* without tanwīn (nunation), considering it a diptote (*mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf*) because of definiteness and feminine gender, interpreting it as a patch of ground (*bugʿa*); or because of *ʿadl* (its form being an altered derivation) from *ṭāwin*; or because of being non-Arabic (*ʿujma*). Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf recite it with tanwīn, considering it the name of a valley which is masculine in its wording.

The clause ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾ (*idhhab ilā Firʿawn*) is an explanation (*bayān*) of the clause ﴿His Lord called to him﴾.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾ (*innahu ṭaghā*) is a reason (*taʿlīl*) for the command in His saying: ﴿Go﴾, and for this reason it is introduced by the particle *inna*, which is for emphasis (*li-l-ihtimām*) and conveys the sense of causation.

The word ﴿ṭughyān﴾ (الطُّغْيانُ) means excessive arrogance. It was discussed previously at His saying: ﴿For the transgressors is a place of return﴾ [al-Naba': 22], in the Chapter of al-Naba'.

The word ﴿Firʿawn﴾ (فِرْعَوْنُ) is the title of the king of the Copts in Egypt in ancient times. It is a word arabized from the Hebrew language. It is not known whether it is a name for the king in the Coptic language. The Qur'an has used it only for the king of Egypt to whom Moses was sent. The name "king" (*al-Malik*) was used for the one in the time of Joseph. The discussion of this was mentioned previously at His saying, ﴿Then We sent after them Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his establishment﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 103], in the Chapter of al-Aʿrāf.

The clause ﴿Is there for you a way to purify yourself, and I would guide you to your Lord?﴾ (*hal laka ilā an tazakkā wa-ahdiyaka ilā rabbika*) is an offer and an encouragement. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech; perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 44].

[p. 75]

The phrase ﴿hal laka﴾ (هَلْ لَكَ) is a construction that has become like a proverb, so it is not altered from this construction, because brevity is intended by it. It is said: *hal laka ilā kadhā?* and *hal laka fī kadhā?* ("Do you have an inclination toward such-and-such?"). It is a statement by which an offer is intended, as a man says to his guest: *hal laka an tanzila?* ("Would you like to descend?"). From the same usage is the saying of Kaʿb:

*"Unquestionably, convey from me a message to Bujayr, / so is there for you in what I have said, may woe be upon you, an inclination?"*

With a *ḍamma* on the *tāʾ* of *qultu*. And the saying of his brother Bujayr in reply to his verses:

*"Who will convey to Kaʿb: is there for you an inclination toward that / for which he blames me falsely, and which is more prudent?"*

The word ﴿laka﴾ (لَكَ) is the predicate of an omitted subject (*khabar mubtadaʾ maḥdhūf*), and its estimated form is: "Is there for you a desire for such-and-such?" So the word "desire" (*raghba*) is omitted and what remains is indicated by the particle *fī*. They also say: "Is there for you an inclination to such-and-such?" on the estimate: "Is there for you a tendency (*mayl*)?" So the word "tendency" is omitted, being indicated by *ilā*.

Al-Ṭībī said: Ibn Jinnī said: Whenever one verb is used in the meaning of another verb, often one of them is treated like its counterpart in usage, so that the usage is made to conform to it and its inflection follows its model, even if the common usage and custom are contrary to its source. Do you not see His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is there for you a way to purify yourself?﴾ whereas you only say: "Is there for you in such-and-such?" But since the meaning of "I take you to such-and-such" or "I call you to it" entered it, He said: ﴿Is there for you a way to purify yourself?﴾ And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to go to your wives (*al-rafath ilā nisāʾikum*)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]: one does not say *rafathtu ilā al-mar'a* ("I had intercourse with the woman"); one says *rafathtu bihā* or *maʿahā*. But since *al-rafath* carried the meaning of *al-ifḍāʾ* (reaching/going to), it was followed by *ilā*. This is one of the most elegant paths of the Arabic language, because it is a place where meaning takes control of the discourse and directs it. End of quotation. It has been said that this is not from the category of *tadmīn* (verb-inclusion), but from the category of metaphor with a linking indicator.

The word ﴿tazakkā﴾ (تَزَكّى) was recited by Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū Jaʿfar, and Yaʿqūb with the *zāy* doubled (shaddah), on the consideration that its original form was *tatazakkā* with two *tāʾs*. The *tāʾ* adjacent to the *zāy* was changed to a *zāy*, because the two articulation points are close, and it was assimilated into the *zāy*. The rest recited it with a single *zāy*, on the basis that one of the two *tāʾs* was deleted for the sake of lightening.

The verb ﴿tazakkā﴾, in both readings, originally is *tatazakkā* with two *tāʾs*, the present form of *tazakkā*, the reflexive of *zakkāhu*, that is, "he made him pure (*zakī*)."

[p. 76]

The word *zakāh* (الزَّكاةُ) means increase, and it is used for increase in inner good, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who corrupts it﴾ [al-Shams: 9]. This is a widespread metaphor which has become equal to the literal meaning, and for this reason it does not require an indicator.

The meaning is: urging him to prepare himself to free his soul from the misguided creed, which is a metaphorical impurity in the soul, so that he accepts the guidance of one who guides him to that by which the good increases. For the reflexive verb form indicates an agent who treats his own soul and trains it, since he had not been guided to purify his soul by himself.

For this reason He followed it with the conjunction: ﴿and I would guide you to your Lord, so you would fear﴾, meaning: if there is in you a preparation of yourself for purification, then my guidance of you will be that you fear. Thus the arrangement of the clauses in mention takes into account their order in occurrence. Therefore it was not necessary to connect them with the particle *fa'* of sequence (*fāʾ al-tafrīʿ*), since the conjunction *wa* (and) is often sufficient, even with the intention of sequence, without a particle of sequence, because *wa* indicates sequence by context. The conjunction may also dispense with mentioning the explanatory particle in explanatory coordination (*al-ʿaṭf al-tafsīrī*), in which *wa* carries the sense of the explanatory *ay*, since ﴿an tazakkā wa-ahdiyaka﴾ is in the force of a single noun. The estimated meaning is: "Is there for you an inclination toward purification and my guidance of you, so that you fear God, the Exalted?"

The word *hidāya* (guidance) means pointing to the path which leads to the sought goal, when the one guided accepts it.

The linking of ﴿fa-takhshā﴾ (فَتَخْشى, "so you fear") to ﴿ahdiyaka﴾ (أهْدِيَكَ, "I guide you") indicates that the fear of God does not occur except through knowledge. He, the Exalted, said: "Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God" [Fāṭir: 28], meaning: those who have knowledge of Him; that is, they fear Him with complete fear, without error or deficiency in it.

Al-Ṭībī said: From al-Wāsiṭī: the beginnings of knowledge are fear, then reverence, then glorification, then awe, then annihilation.

In restricting the mention to fear there is eloquent brevity, because fear is the foundation of every good. In the *Jāmiʿ* of al-Tirmidhī, from Abū Hurayra, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Whoever fears sets out early by night, and whoever sets out early by night reaches the destination."

[p. 77]

The true God is mentioned to him by the attribute of "your Lord" (*rabbika*), without mentioning the proper name God (Allāh) or any other form of definition, out of gentleness in the call to monotheism, and to avoid making his soul flee in aversion. For in the language of Pharaoh the name of God the Exalted was not known, and if Moses had defined Him to him by His name in the language of the Israelites, he would have repelled. For Pharaoh used to worship false gods. So in His saying "to your Lord" (while Pharaoh knew that he had a lord), there was an enticement to him that Moses might guide him to what does not contradict his beliefs, so that he would listen to him, until when he heard his words and his argument, true faith would enter him gradually. In this method there is a drawing down of his bird (i.e., gently bringing him down from his height).

The word *khashya* (الخَشْيَةُ) means fear. When it is used in the language of the Sharīʿa (divine law), what is meant by it is fear of God, the Exalted. For this reason its verb here is treated as intransitive, so no object is mentioned, because the object of fear is known. It is like the verb *īmān* (faith) in the language of the Sharīʿa. It is said: "So-and-so believed," and "So-and-so is a believer," meaning: a believer in God and in His oneness.

The purpose is that the mention of the story of Moses should bring consolation to the Messenger ﷺ and admonition to the polytheists and their leaders, such as Abu Jahl, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and their likes, in accordance with His saying at its end: ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for those who fear﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26].

Thus it makes no difference whether he knew it before or not. For this reason the speaker does not wait for an answer from the one addressed; rather, he follows the interrogative with a detailed account of what the interrogative had left vague, as a way of indicating the importance of the report, to the point that it is something people ask about.

The commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 79, verses 20–24:

﴿So he showed him the greatest sign﴾ ﴿but he denied and disobeyed﴾ ﴿then he turned away, striving﴾ ﴿then he gathered [his people] and called out﴾ ﴿and said, "I am your lord, the Most High."﴾

The fa' in His words ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign﴾ is fasihah (the fa' that signals an unstated antecedent), and it introduces a consequence of an omitted clause implied by His words ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 17]. The implied meaning is: he went, called him, and he denied him, so he showed him the greatest sign. This is because His words "Indeed, he has transgressed" (innahu taghā) indicate that he would meet Musa's call with contempt and denial, since transgression (al-tughyan) is the usual cause of both. So Musa proposed that he display a sign that proves the truth of his call, perhaps he would become certain, as God said: ﴿He said, "Even if I brought you something clear?"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 30] ﴿He said, "Then bring it, if you should be of the truthful."﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 31] ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clear serpent.﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 32] That is the greatest sign intended here.

Ayah (āyah): its literal meaning is sign or indication. It is applied to a proof that establishes something, since it is a sign of the establishment of the truth, and it is applied to the miracle of a messenger, since it is evidence of the messenger's truthfulness, which is what is meant here.

The act of ﴿showing him the greatest sign﴾ is followed by the verb (fa-kadhdhaba, "so he denied"), to indicate the intensity of his obstinacy and arrogance, to the extent that he saw the sign yet did not hesitate or pause to consider its implication, but rushed to denial and disobedience.

What is meant by his disobedience is disobeying God's command that he worship Him alone, or that he release the Children of Israel from their enslavement and their being forced to serve in his lands.

The conjunction of ﴿then he turned away, striving﴾ with (thumma, "then") indicates graduated succession (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), as is its usage in conjoining sentences. Thumma conveys that the content of the sentence it conjoins is higher in rank with respect to the purpose contained in the preceding sentence; that is, he advanced from denial and disobedience to something more severe, namely turning away, striving, and claiming divinity for himself. That is: after reflecting at length, he was not persuaded by mere denial and disobedience, and he feared that if he remained silent, Musa's call might spread among the people, so he sought to take precaution to repel it and warn the people against it.

The words "turning away" (idbar) and "striving" (sa'y) are both used in their figurative senses. The literal meaning of idbar is walking in the direction behind the walker, by turning to one direction and then turning to the opposite. Here it is metaphorically used for turning away from the call of the one who calls, like the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Musaylimah when he refused to believe: "And if you turn away, God will surely destroy you."

As for sa'y, its literal meaning is intense walking, and here it is metaphorically used for eagerness and diligence in commanding the people not to listen to Musa's words, and in gathering the magicians to oppose his miracle, since he considered it magic, as God said: ﴿So Pharaoh turned away and gathered his schemes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 60].

The action toward which he strove is explained by His words: ﴿Then he gathered [his people] and called out﴾ ﴿and said, "I am your lord, the Most High."﴾ All three are arranged as consequences of sa'y.

The clause ﴿then he gathered﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿striving﴾, because Pharaoh exerted his effort to convince his subjects that he was the Most High Lord, fearing the spread of Musa's call to worship the true Lord.

It is also possible that (adbar) is meant in its literal sense, that is: he left that assembly by standing up turned away, announcing his anger at Musa, and (yas'a) is also used in its literal sense: he rose, walking briskly, which is the gait of one who is angry and turning away.

The word al-hashr means gathering people, and this gathering is the one explained in His words: ﴿They said, "Put him off, and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 36] ﴿who will bring you every learned magician"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 37].

The object of (hashara) is omitted because it is evident, since those who are gathered are the people of his city from every class.

The coordination of (fa-nada, "so he called out") with fa' indicates that he announced this statement to them immediately upon their presence, out of his intense eagerness to convey it to them.

Al-nida' (calling out): its literal meaning is raising the voice to summon someone to attend, and for this reason the particles of address act as a substitute for ʾadʿū ("I call"), so they put in the accusative the noun that follows them. Al-nida' is also applied to raising the voice without summoning someone to attend, as a metonymy by a relation of necessity, like al-Hariri's words in the thirtieth maqamah: "When he sat down, as if he were the son of the rain-water, a caller called out from the direction of the in-laws," etc. The object of (nada) is omitted just as the object of (hashara) was omitted.

Attributing the gathering and the calling out to Pharaoh is a rational metonymy (majaz ʿaqli), because he does not personally gather the people or call to them, but orders his followers and soldiers to do so. It is attributed to him because he is the one who commanded it, like the saying: "al-Mansur built Baghdad."

The statement with which he called out is a reminder to his people of their belief about him, for they regarded the king of Egypt as a god, because the priests told them that he was the son of Amun-Ra, whom they regard as a god and whose manifestation is the sun.

The restrictive form in (anā rabbukum, "I am your lord") is in response to Musa's call.

His words ﴿and said, "I am your lord, the Most High."﴾ are an exact substitute (badal mutabiq) for the clause (fa-nada), with the conjunction restated, namely fa'; because the substitute may be accompanied by a particle similar to the governing element of the substituted-from element, for the purpose of emphasis, as in His words: ﴿And from the palm, from its spathe, hanging clusters near﴾ [al-An'am: 99], and this was discussed in Surat al-An'am.

It is also possible that the clause ﴿So he said, "I am your lord"﴾ is coordinated with the clause (yas'a), on the basis that Pharaoh ordered this statement to be made throughout the regions of his kingdom, and it was not confined to proclaiming it to those gathered around his palace.

He described himself as "the Most High Lord" because he was the son of Amun-Ra, who is the Most High Lord, so his son is the one who carries that attribute; or because in the age of their belief, Pharaoh was regarded as the lord of the many lords they had, so the attribute "the Most High" is a clarifying attribute.

The act of ﴿showing him the greatest sign﴾ is followed by the verb (fa-kadhdhaba, "so he denied"), to indicate the intensity of his obstinacy and arrogance, to the extent that he saw the sign yet did not hesitate or pause to consider its implication, but rushed to denial and disobedience.

What is meant by his disobedience is disobeying God's command that he worship Him alone, or that he release the Children of Israel from their enslavement and their being forced to serve in his lands.

The conjunction of ﴿then he turned away, striving﴾ with (thumma, "then") indicates graduated succession (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), as is its usage in conjoining sentences. Thumma conveys that the content of the sentence it conjoins is higher in rank with respect to the purpose contained in the preceding sentence; that is, he advanced from denial and disobedience to something more severe, namely turning away, striving, and claiming divinity for himself. That is: after reflecting at length, he was not persuaded by mere denial and disobedience, and he feared that if he remained silent, Musa's call might spread among the people, so he sought to take precaution to repel it and warn the people against it.

The words "turning away" (idbar) and "striving" (sa'y) are both used in their figurative senses. The literal meaning of idbar is walking in the direction behind the walker, by turning to one direction and then turning to the opposite. Here it is metaphorically used for turning away from the call of the one who calls, like the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Musaylimah when he refused to believe: "And if you turn away, God will surely destroy you."

As for sa'y, its literal meaning is intense walking, and here it is metaphorically used for eagerness and diligence in commanding the people not to listen to Musa's words, and in gathering the magicians to oppose his miracle, since he considered it magic, as God said: ﴿So Pharaoh turned away and gathered his schemes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 60].

The action toward which he strove is explained by His words: ﴿Then he gathered [his people] and called out﴾ ﴿and said, "I am your lord, the Most High."﴾ All three are arranged as consequences of sa'y.

The clause ﴿then he gathered﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿striving﴾, because Pharaoh exerted his effort to convince his subjects that he was the Most High Lord, fearing the spread of Musa's call to worship the true Lord.

It is also possible that (adbar) is meant in its literal sense, that is: he left that assembly by standing up turned away, announcing his anger at Musa, and (yas'a) is also used in its literal sense: he rose, walking briskly, which is the gait of one who is angry and turning away.

The word al-hashr means gathering people, and this gathering is the one explained in His words: ﴿They said, "Put him off, and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 36] ﴿who will bring you every learned magician"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 37].

The object of (hashara) is omitted because it is evident, since those who are gathered are the people of his city from every class.

The coordination of (fa-nada, "so he called out") with fa' indicates that he announced this statement to them immediately upon their presence, out of his intense eagerness to convey it to them.

Al-nida' (calling out): its literal meaning is raising the voice to summon someone to attend, and for this reason the particles of address act as a substitute for ʾadʿū ("I call"), so they put in the accusative the noun that follows them. Al-nida' is also applied to raising the voice without summoning someone to attend, as a metonymy by a relation of necessity, like al-Hariri's words in the thirtieth maqamah: "When he sat down, as if he were the son of the rain-water, a caller called out from the direction of the in-laws," etc. The object of (nada) is omitted just as the object of (hashara) was omitted.

Attributing the gathering and the calling out to Pharaoh is a rational metonymy (majaz ʿaqli), because he does not personally gather the people or call to them, but orders his followers and soldiers to do so. It is attributed to him because he is the one who commanded it, like the saying: "al-Mansur built Baghdad."

The statement with which he called out is a reminder to his people of their belief about him, for they regarded the king of Egypt as a god, because the priests told them that he was the son of Amun-Ra, whom they regard as a god and whose manifestation is the sun.

The restrictive form in (anā rabbukum, "I am your lord") is in response to Musa's call.

His words ﴿and said, "I am your lord, the Most High."﴾ are an exact substitute (badal mutabiq) for the clause (fa-nada), with the conjunction restated, namely fa'; because the substitute may be accompanied by a particle similar to the governing element of the substituted-from element, for the purpose of emphasis, as in His words: ﴿And from the palm, from its spathe, hanging clusters near﴾ [al-An'am: 99], and this was discussed in Surat al-An'am.

It is also possible that the clause ﴿So he said, "I am your lord"﴾ is coordinated with the clause (yas'a), on the basis that Pharaoh ordered this statement to be made throughout the regions of his kingdom, and it was not confined to proclaiming it to those gathered around his palace.

He described himself as "the Most High Lord" because he was the son of Amun-Ra, who is the Most High Lord, so his son is the one who carries that attribute; or because in the age of their belief, Pharaoh was regarded as the lord of the many lords they had, so the attribute "the Most High" is a clarifying attribute.

[Page 81]

The clause ﴿So Allah seized him as an example for the Hereafter and the former﴾ is a consequence (*mufarra'ah*) of the clauses preceding it. That is, what was mentioned of his denial, his disobedience, and his scheming was the cause of Allah seizing him. This is the purpose of relating the story, and it is the basis for admonishing and warning the polytheists, along with consoling and strengthening the Prophet ﷺ.

The literal meaning of *al-akhdh* (seizing) is taking hold with the hand. It is frequently used metaphorically for power and dominance, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We seized them, the seizure of One Mighty and Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 42], and He said: ﴿So He seized them with a overwhelming seizure﴾ [al-Haqqah: 10]. The meaning is: he did not escape the punishment of Allah.

*Al-nakal* is a verbal noun of *nakkala bihi tankeelan*, and it is like *al-salam* in meaning *al-taslim*. The meaning of *al-nakal* is inflicting severe harm upon another, by publicizing it in such a way that it deters (*yunakkilu*), i.e., turns back and repels, whoever witnesses it from doing the same as what the one punished was subjected to. It is derived from *al-nukul*, which is recoiling and fleeing. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We made it an example for what was before it and what came after it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 66], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The word (نَكالَ) is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*, an object that is a verbal noun of the same root, here used to specify the type of the verb) of the verb (أخَذَهُ), specifying the kind of seizing by two of its kinds, because seizing occurs in many states.

The construct (إضافَةُ) of (نَكالَ) to (الآخِرَةِ والأُولى) is in the sense of (في), meaning "in."

So the punishment in the first life is drowning, and the punishment in the Hereafter is the torment of Hell.

*Al-nakal* has been used in both its literal and figurative senses. What befell Pharaoh in this world was a real punishment, while what he will suffer in the Hereafter was called *nakal* because it resembles punishment in the severity of torment, though it does not produce deterrence on the Day of Resurrection.

The verb (أخَذَهُ) appears in the past tense, although the punishment of the Hereafter is future relative to the Day of Recompense. This is taken into account in that when he died, he began to taste the punishment, when he sees his position to which he will return on the Day of Recompense, as is related in the hadith.

The mention of (الآخِرَةِ) before the first is because the matter of the Hereafter is greater.

At the end of the story comes a summary and conclusion of what preceded, so He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾. It has the sense of clarifying the content of the clause ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 15] and what follows.

The demonstrative in His saying "in that" refers to the story of Moses.

*Al-'ibrah* (lesson) is a state by which the mind passes from knowing it to knowing its consequence or the consequence of its like. It is derived from *al-'abr*, which is crossing from one bank of a valley or river to its other bank.

What is meant by *al-'ibrah* here is admonition (*maw'izah*).

The indefiniteness of (عِبْرَةً) is for magnification, because in this story there are many admonitions from various aspects, which are examples for deeds and their consequences, and of watchfulness over Allah and fear of Him, and what follows from that and from its opposite of good and evil in this world and the Hereafter. That is made a lesson for "whoever fears," meaning whose soul is mingled with the fear of Allah, because those who fear Allah are the people of knowledge who understand the indication of things by their necessary implications and hidden meanings. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28], and He said: ﴿And these are the parables We present to the people, but none understands them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43]. The fear (*al-khashyah*) was mentioned shortly before in His saying: ﴿And I will guide you to your Lord so you will fear Him﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 19].

In this there is an allusion to the polytheists, that they are not fit to benefit from the like of this, just as Pharaoh and his people did not benefit from its like.

Throughout the whole story there is an allusion to the chiefs of Quraysh among the disbelievers, such as Abu Jahl, by comparing them to Pharaoh, and comparing the common people to the people whom Pharaoh gathered and called to disbelief. The Muslims knew the target of this example, so Abu Jahl was described among the Muslims as the Pharaoh of this community.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 79, verses 27–29:

﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is it the sky? He built it.﴾ ﴿He raised its vault and made it even.﴾ ﴿And He darkened its night and brought out its forenoon.﴾

A transition from the admonition by the examples of past nations, which is a warning and threat against their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), to refuting their doubt about the denial of resurrection, which is their saying: ﴿Shall we indeed be returned to our former state?﴾ and what they followed it with of mockery, based on the supposition that resurrection is impossible. Since they assumed the impossibility of returning life to decayed bodies, by taking their own bodies as the example, when they said ﴿Shall we indeed be returned?﴾, the refutation of their doubt came by comparing the creation of their bodies with the creation of the heavens and the earth, and so it was said to them: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is it the sky?﴾. Therefore it was said to them here "Are you" with their own pronoun, and it was not said "Is man the more difficult to create?", though they are only from mankind. So the address is directed to the polytheists who were referred to a little earlier with third-person pronouns, from His saying "they say" up to His saying: ﴿then they will be at the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 14], and this is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person.

So the sentence is resumed (mustanaf'a) for the purpose of answering their doubt, because the report of their doubt with "they say: Shall we indeed..." up to its end requires the expectation of an answer to that saying, as the allusion to it was previously made at His saying: "they say: Shall we indeed be returned?"

The interrogation is rhetorical (taqriri). The purpose of the affirmation is to compel them to acknowledge that the creation of the sky is greater than their creation, that is, greater than the creation of their kind, which is the human kind, and they know that Allah is the Creator of the sky. Thus there is no doubt that He who is capable of creating the sky is capable of creating man a second time. This yields that the re-creation of bodies after their annihilation is within Allah's power, since He is capable of what is greater than that. He, Exalted, said: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most of mankind do not know﴾ [Ghafir: 57]. That is because their rational sight was clouded by habit, so they considered what they were not accustomed to to be impossible, and did not turn their attention to the possibility of what is greater than what they deemed impossible.

"Ashadd" (أشدّ) is a superlative, and the thing it is compared to is omitted, indicated by His saying "or is it the sky" (أم السماء).
The meaning of "ashadd" is "more difficult" (aṣ'ab), and "khalqan" (خلقاً) is a verbal noun in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of the attribution of greater difficulty to them, that is: "Are you more difficult in terms of Allah's creating you, or is His creating the sky?" So the specification is transferred from the subject.

"Al-sama'" (السماء) may mean the genus, and its definiteness is the definiteness of the genus, that is, the heavens, which are hidden from human observation; so the rhetorical interrogation is based on what is well known among people of the greatness of the heavens, treating the intelligible as if it were the perceptible.

It may also mean a specific sky, namely the one called the lowest sky, in which the lights of the stars appear; its definiteness is then the definiteness of prior reference. It is the spherical atmosphere surrounding the earth, in which the light of day and the darkness of night appear. The rhetorical interrogation is then based on what is observed by them. This is more suitable with His saying: ﴿And He darkened its night and brought out its forenoon﴾, since it does not need interpretation.

The clause "banaha" (بناها) may be a resumed sentence (istinaf bayani), explaining the strength of the creation of the sky, and it may be a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for His saying "or is it the sky", since it is in the sense of: "or is the sky more difficult to create?" The word "banaha" has been made a verse-end (fasilah), so the pause is at it, and there is no harm in that, since there is no ambiguity in the meaning; because "banaha" is a clause, and the equalizing "am" is not followed except by a single noun.

Building (al-binā'): making a house or dwelling of stone, or brick, or leather, or cloths of woven hair, whose pieces are fastened to one another by stitching or sewing and set up on supports. What is of leather is called a qubba (dome), and what is of cloth is called a khayma (tent) and khibā' (tent).

The building of the sky is its creation; the verb of building is borrowed for it because the sky resembles houses in height.

The clause "raised its vault and made it even" explains the clause "banaha", or is a substitution of inclusion from it. The method of summary followed by detail was taken to increase the depiction.

Al-samk (السمك), with a fatha on the sīn and a sukūn on the mīm: elevation in space, as al-Raghib limited it, whether the raised thing is connected to the earth or not; it is the verbal noun of samaka. Al-raf' (الرفع): making a body elevated, and it is synonymous with al-samk, so the transitivity of the verb "raised" to "samk" is for emphasis on the elevation, that is: "He raised its elevation," meaning He made it lofty, and it is of the type of their saying: "laylun alyal" (a very dark night), "shi'run sha'ir" (a poem that is truly poetic), and "zillun zalil" (a very deep shade).

Al-taswiyah (التسوية): equalization and absence of disparity, and it is making things equal, that is, similar; its origin is that it relates to things, and it may relate to the name of a single thing in the sense of equalizing its directions and sides. From this is His saying here "fasawwaha", that is, He equalized its parts, by perfecting its making, so you do not see in it any disparity.

The "fa" in "fasawwaha" is for sequence (ta'qib).

The equalization of the sky occurred together with the occurrence of its elevation, so the sequence in it is like the sequence in His saying: ﴿then he called﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 23] ﴿and said: I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24].

The clause "and He darkened its night" is coordinated with the clause "banaha", and is not coordinated with "raised its vault", because darkening the night and bringing out the forenoon are not among the things by which building is explained.

Al-ighṭāsh (الإغطاش): making it dark, that is, gloom; it is said: "ghatasha al-layl" (ghatasha, of the pattern daraba), meaning it became dark.

The meaning: He singled out the night for darkness and made it gloomy, that is, He made its night dark, and this is close to His saying "raised its vault", in the manner of their saying "laylun alyal".

Ikhrāj al-ḍuḥā (إخراج الضحى): bringing forth the light of the forenoon. The original sense of ikhrāj is removal from a containing place, and it is borrowed for manifestation by a common metaphor.

Al-ḍuḥā (الضحى): the emergence of the light of the sun after its rising and after its rays have reddened; so ḍuḥā is the pure light of the sun, and its time was named by it, by supposing an omitted genitive, as in His saying, Exalted: ﴿and that people be gathered at forenoon﴾ [Ta-Ha: 59]. What supports this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿By the sun and its ḍuḥā﴾ [al-Shams: 1], that is, its clear light.

It is because the manifestation of light was made "ikhrāj" (bringing out) that light arises after darkness, since darkness is an absence and it is prior, while light needs a cause that illuminates it.

The attribution of "layl" and "ḍuḥā" to the pronoun of the sky: if the sky is the lowest sky, then it is because both appear to people in the atmosphere of the sky, so the forenoon appears as rays spreading from the sky, proceeding from the direction of the sunrise, so the rays fall on the face of the earth; then when the sun is hidden by the earth's rotation in the day and night, darkness begins to take the place of what contracts of the sun's rays on the horizon, until it becomes a pitch-black night enveloping a part of the terrestrial sphere.

If "al-sama'" is a genus for the heavens, then the attribution of "layl" and "ḍuḥā" to the heavens is because both appear in their directions.

Al-taswiyah (التسوية): equalization and absence of disparity, and it is making things equal, that is, similar; its origin is that it relates to things, and it may relate to the name of a single thing in the sense of equalizing its directions and sides. From this is His saying here "fasawwaha", that is, He equalized its parts, by perfecting its making, so you do not see in it any disparity.

The "fa" in "fasawwaha" is for sequence (ta'qib).

The equalization of the sky occurred together with the occurrence of its elevation, so the sequence in it is like the sequence in His saying: ﴿then he called﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 23] ﴿and said: I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24].

The clause "and He darkened its night" is coordinated with the clause "banaha", and is not coordinated with "raised its vault", because darkening the night and bringing out the forenoon are not among the things by which building is explained.

The meaning: He singled out the night for darkness and made it gloomy, that is, He made its night dark, and this is close to His saying "raised its vault", in the manner of their saying "laylun alyal".

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 79, verses 27–29:

A transition from the admonition by the examples of past nations, which is a warning and threat against their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), to refuting their doubt about the denial of resurrection, which is their saying: ﴿Shall we indeed be returned to our former state?﴾ and what they followed it with of mockery, based on the supposition that resurrection is impossible. Since they assumed the impossibility of returning life to decayed bodies, by taking their own bodies as the example, when they said ﴿Shall we indeed be returned?﴾, the refutation of their doubt came by comparing the creation of their bodies with the creation of the heavens and the earth, and so it was said to them: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is it the sky?﴾. Therefore it was said to them here "Are you" with their own pronoun, and it was not said "Is man the more difficult to create?", though they are only from mankind. So the address is directed to the polytheists who were referred to a little earlier with third-person pronouns, from His saying "they say" up to His saying: ﴿then they will be at the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 14], and this is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person.

So the sentence is resumed (mustanaf'a) for the purpose of answering their doubt, because the report of their doubt with "they say: Shall we indeed..." up to its end requires the expectation of an answer to that saying, as the allusion to it was previously made at His saying: "they say: Shall we indeed be returned?"

The interrogation is rhetorical (taqriri). The purpose of the affirmation is to compel them to acknowledge that the creation of the sky is greater than their creation, that is, greater than the creation of their kind, which is the human kind, and they know that Allah is the Creator of the sky. Thus there is no doubt that He who is capable of creating the sky is capable of creating man a second time. This yields that the re-creation of bodies after their annihilation is within Allah's power, since He is capable of what is greater than that. He, Exalted, said: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most of mankind do not know﴾ [Ghafir: 57]. That is because their rational sight was clouded by habit, so they considered what they were not accustomed to to be impossible, and did not turn their attention to the possibility of what is greater than what they deemed impossible.

So the specification is transferred from the subject.

It may also mean a specific sky, namely the one called the lowest sky, in which the lights of the stars appear; its definiteness is then the definiteness of prior reference. It is the spherical atmosphere surrounding the earth, in which the light of day and the darkness of night appear. The rhetorical interrogation is then based on what is observed by them. What is of leather is called a qubba (dome), and what is of cloth is called a khayma (tent) and khibā' (tent).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 79, verses 30–32:

﴿And the earth—after that He spread it out.﴾ ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture.﴾ ﴿And the mountains He set firmly.﴾

The discourse shifted from argument by the creation of the heaven to argument by the creation of the earth, because the earth is closer to their observation, and what is found upon the earth is closer to their knowledge, in detail or in a general manner close to detail.

Out of concern for the indication of the creation of the earth and what it contains, the noun "al-ard" (the earth) was placed before its verb and its subject, so it was put in the accusative by the method of al-ishtighal (the verb-occupied construction, in which a verb is elided and its object is represented by a pronoun). Al-ishtighal includes emphasis, in view of the implied verb governing the topicalised noun, indicated by the apparent verb occupied with the pronoun of the fronted noun.

Al-dahw and al-dahy are both said: dahawtu and dahaytu. Al-Jawhari restricted it to the waw form, and it is the form prevalent in the speech of the exegetes. It means: spreading and extending with levelling.

The meaning: He created it spread out (madhuwwatan), that is, extended and levelled.

The reference in His words "after that" (ba'da dhalika) is to what is understood from ﴿He raised its height and made it level﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27], that is: after He created the heaven, He created the earth spread out.

Page 87
The sense of "after" (al-ba'diyyah) apparently denotes the lateness of the time in which the act occurs. This verse is more evident in indicating that the earth was created after the heavens, and this is the view of Qatadah, Muqatil, and al-Suddi, and it is what the evidences of the science of astronomy support. This was explained earlier at His words: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth; then He turned to the heaven and made it seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29] in Surat al-Baqarah. As for the verses whose apparent meaning resembles the apparent meaning of the verse in Surat al-Baqarah, their interpretation is clear.
It is permissible that "ba'd" be figurative, denoting the descent in rank of what "ba'd" is attached to from the rank of what was mentioned before it, as in His words: ﴿Then, after that, a rough-natured, base-born one﴾ [al-Qalam: 13].

The clause ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause "dahaha", because the purpose of its spreading is, by necessity, that which completes the facilitation of benefiting from it.

It is not valid to make the clause ﴿He brought forth from it its water…﴾ to its end an explanation (bayan) of the clause "dahaha", because the two verbs differ in meaning.

Al-mar'a (pasture): a noun of place from ra'a yar'a, and here it is a mimi verbal noun used for the thing acted upon, like "al-khalq" in the sense of "al-makhluq" (the created thing). That is: He brought forth from it what is grazed.

Al-ra'y (grazing) in its reality is the animals' taking of herbage, grass, and green fodder.

So restricting the mention to pasture suffices instead of mentioning what the earth brings forth of fruits and grains, because mentioning pasture indicates God's kindness to the animals, from which it is known that kindness to humans is more fitting, by the indication of the implication of the discourse. The indicator of this sufficiency is His saying after it: ﴿as a provision for you and for your cattle﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 33].

By mentioning water and pasture, He has indicated all that the earth brings forth as food for people and animals, even the firewood with which food is cooked, for it is among what the earth grows, and even salt, for it is from the water that is upon the earth.

The accusative of "al-jibal" (the mountains) may be by the method of the accusative of ﴿And the earth—after that He spread it out﴾; it may also be a conjunction upon ﴿its water and its pasture﴾, and the meaning would be: and He brought forth from it its mountains, so "al" is a substitute for the genitive-attached noun, like: ﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 41], that is: the refuge of one who feared the standing before his Lord. Indeed the mountains are pieces of the earth projecting upon the surface of the earth.

Page 88
The setting (irsa') of the mountains is their being fixed in the earth. It is said: the ship came to rest (rasat al-safinah) when it was tied to the shore and stopped at the anchor. The mountain is described with rusuww (being firmly fixed) in its literal sense, as in al-Asas. Al-Samaw'al, or 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Abd al-Rahim, said, mentioning their mountain:

Its root is settled above the soil, and it rose with a summit unreachable, tall, toward the stars.

The fixing of the mountains is their firm rootedness through the penetration of their rocks and the roots of their trees, for they were created with rocks extending down into the interior of the earth; were it not so, the winds would have shaken them. They were created with rocks and trees interlacing within them; were it not so, their soil would have crumbled. Added to this is that their sizes were made proportionate, being created broad at the base and then rising, narrowing as they ascend.
From the meaning of their setting is that they were made sloping so that people may climb them with ease, just as a rider can board a ship that is anchored; and had they been in the depths of the sea, one could not board them except with hardship.
