The verb refers back to the creation of the earth and the mountains. In the case of the earth this is evident. As for the mountains, they are their refuge from their enemies, and in them are the pastures of their livestock, which are safe in the mountains from raids upon them by surprise. This is an **idmaj al-imtinan** (interweaving of the favour into the argument) to stir up their gratitude for the favour due to it, by worshipping the Benefactor alone and not associating anything else with His worship.

In His words, ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30] up to *(wa-li-anʿamikum)*, there is a **muhassin al-jamʿ thumma al-taqsim** (the embellishment of gathering followed by division).

[Page 89]

﴿So when the Great Catastrophe comes﴾ ﴿On the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ ﴿And Hellfire is brought forth for whoever sees﴾ ﴿As for him who transgressed﴾ ﴿And preferred the worldly life﴾ ﴿Indeed, Hellfire will be his refuge﴾ ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire﴾ ﴿Indeed, Paradise will be his refuge﴾.

It is possible that this is a consequence (tafri') of the argument contained in His saying: ﴿Are you more difficult to create or is the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27] and what follows it. For the establishment of resurrection necessitates recompense, since recompense is its wisdom. When recompense is necessitated, it is incumbent upon the rational person to act for the reward of the good (al-husna), to avoid what leads to wretchedness, to care for the everlasting life and prefer it, and not to be indifferent to a transient bliss so as to become entangled in pursuing it. Therefore, after the proof for the establishment of resurrection, there follows a reminder of the two recompenses and guidance toward the two paths (al-najdayn).

Since a general warning had already been given before the argument, in His saying: ﴿On the day when the quaking one quakes﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 6] and what follows, just as the thesis (al-matlub) is mentioned before the syllogism (qiyas) in dialectic (jadal), after the argument there came a detailed explanation of that warning, combined with good tidings for whoever adorns himself with its opposite. Therefore resurrection is expressed at the outset as "the quaking one" because it is its beginning, then as "the blast" (al-zajra), and finally as "the Great Catastrophe" (al-tammah al-kubra), because these two descriptions contain a meaning that encompasses the quaking and the terrors that follow it until each party settles in its abode.

And among the completeness of the appropriateness (munasaba) for reminding of the Day of Recompense is that it comes after the reminder of the creation of the earth and the favour of what He prepared from it for man as provision, indicating that this provision ends when the Day of Resurrection and Recompense arrives.

It is also possible to make His saying: ﴿So when the Great Catastrophe comes﴾ a consequence of His saying: ﴿It is but one blast﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 13] ﴿and at once they are on the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 14], for the Catastrophe is the Blast.

The basis of the consequence (manat al-tafri') is what follows it of detail in His saying: ﴿As for him who transgressed﴾ and so on, for it is not appropriate for a thing to be made a consequence of itself.

The particle (idha) denotes the future, so when it is followed by a past-tense verb, it is turned toward the future. The past tense is used after (idha) only to increase the confirmation of what (idha) conveys of the certainty of occurrence.

Al-majiy' (coming) here is a metaphor (majaz) for occurrence and taking place, because a thing fixed and deferred to a term resembles a person travelling toward a goal; when that deferred thing arrives at its appointed time, it is as if the traveller has reached the intended place.

Al-tammah (the Catastrophe) is the event or calamity that overwhelms (tamm), i.e., rises high and prevails, meaning it surpasses its like within its kind such that its equal is rare in its kind. It is derived from "tamma al-ma'" (the water overflowed) when it covers things. This description indicates severity and terror, for such a term is used only for dreadful matters. Then its dreadfulness is emphasised by describing it as "the Great" (al-kubra), and this is the clearest of expressions for depicting the terrors that accompany the event.

What is meant by "the Great Catastrophe" is the Resurrection, and it has been described in the Qur'an with many attributes, such as "the Deafening Blast" (al-sakhkha), "the Striking Calamity" (al-qari'a), "the Quaking" (al-raji'a), and it has been described as "the Great."

His saying: ﴿On the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the clause ﴿So when the Great Catastrophe comes﴾, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because what is added to the word "day" is one of the circumstances that the time of the arrival of the Catastrophe, which is the Day of Resurrection and the Day of Reckoning, includes. And man's remembering what he strove for means that his deeds in his record are presented to him, because "tadhakkur" (remembering) is the reflexive form (mutawi') of "dhakkara" (to cause to remember).

Remembering presupposes a prior forgetting, which is the effacement of what was known from the memory.

The meaning is: on the day he is reminded and so he remembers, that is, his deed is presented to him and he acknowledges it, for the purpose of remembering is nothing but its effect, which is the recompense. So remembering is used as a metonymy (kinaya) for recompense. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Read your record; sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾ [al-Isra': 14].

Tabriz al-jahim (the bringing forth of Hellfire) means its being displayed to its inhabitants. The verb in its doubled form (al-fi'l al-mudda'af) is used to convey the display of Hellfire, because it is a display for the purpose of terrifying.

Al-jahim is Jahannam. For this reason its verb is joined to the feminine ta' marbuta, because Jahannam is feminine in usage, or it is understood as "al-nar" (the Fire). Al-jahim is every great fire in a deep pit.

The verb "burrizat" is in the passive voice, because the identity of the one who brings it forth is not the purpose, since the admonition lies in informing of the occurrence of its being brought forth on that day.

As for His saying ﴿for whoever sees﴾, that is, for every seer, the verb "yara" (sees) is treated as intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lazim), because what is intended is "for whoever has sight," as in the saying of al-Buhturi:

"That the one who sees may see, and the one who hears, may listen."

The fa' in His saying ﴿As for him who transgressed﴾ is a link (rabita) for the response of (idha), because the clause "who transgressed" to its end is a nominal clause that contains no verb to which (idha) is attached, so there was no lexical connection between (idha) and its response. Therefore the fa' is brought in to link the response in the surface wording. As for meaning, it is known that (idha) is an adverb that is attached to the sense of stability that lies between the subject and the predicate.

(Amma) is a particle of detail and conditionality, because it carries the sense of "whatever may be the case."

Transgression (al-tughyan) has had its meaning mentioned just before, and what is meant here is that he transgressed against the command of Allah, as indicated by His saying: ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾.

The mention of transgression was placed before preferring the worldly life, because transgression is among the greatest causes of preferring the worldly life. Since it is the cause of it, it is mentioned right after it, observing the natural order.

Preference (al-iytar) is to prefer one thing over another in a state where it is not possible to combine the conditions of both.

The verb of preference is transitively extended to the object preferred by directly taking its object, and it is extended to the thing it is preferred over by the particle "ʿala" (over). Allah the Exalted said, relating: ﴿Indeed, Allah has preferred you over us﴾ [Yusuf: 91]. The mention of what is preferred over may be omitted when the mention of the preferred thing points to it, as when the preferred and the preferred-over are opposites, as here, due to the common contrast between the worldly life and the Hereafter.

The mention of the preferred may also be omitted, being satisfied with the mention of what is preferred over, when that is the more important, as in His saying: ﴿And they prefer [others] over themselves﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], since it is evident that what is meant is that they prefer "the poor."

[Page 90]

What is meant by "the worldly life" is its portions and benefits specific to it, that is, those that the portions of the Hereafter do not share with it. So the speech is with an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf), its estimated form being: "the bliss of the life."

It is understood from the verb of preference that with it there is a rejection of the bliss of the Hereafter. The preference for the worldly life returns to the satisfaction of the soul's desire, and both portions are known only through divine stipulation, just as shirk, the denial of the messengers, aggression against people, insolence, arrogance, and what follows from these of blameworthy states are known.

The essence of this preference is transgression against the command of Allah, for their leaders and those who direct them know that what the Messenger calls them to is the truth, but they hate following him out of arrogance, refusing to become followers of others, lest their dominion be lost. This meaning is further clarified by His saying after it: ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ and so on. From this it becomes clear that the basis of blame in preferring the worldly life is preferring it over the Hereafter. As for taking from the portions of the worldly life, which taking them does not forfeit the portions of the Hereafter, that is not blameworthy, and it is the station of many of the righteous servants of Allah, which Allah the Exalted relates about the righteous among the Children of Israel, in their saying to Qarun: ﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your portion of the world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77].

His saying ﴿who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ is the counterpart of His saying "who transgressed," because fear is the opposite of transgression. And His saying ﴿and restrained the soul from desire﴾ is the counterpart of His saying ﴿and preferred the worldly life﴾.

The restraining of the fearful person of his soul is used metaphorically (isti'ara) for refraining from taking what the soul loves of sins and desires. So the human soul is made like another person who calls him to evil deeds while he forbids him from this call. This resembles what is called "tajrid" (abstraction), as they say: "his soul told him such-and-such, so he disobeyed it," and it is said: "he forbade his heart." Among the finest of what has been said in this regard is the saying of 'Urwa ibn Udhayna:

"When I find for it whispers of consolation,
the heart interceded with the conscience, so it stilled it."

What is meant by "desire" (al-hawa) is what the soul desires. It is a verbal noun in the sense of the object, like "khalq" in the sense of "makhluq" (created thing). It is what the appetitive and irascible powers of the soul incline toward, of what opposes the truth and complete benefit. Desire has become common in reference to blameworthy inclinations, and for this reason it has been said regarding His saying:

[Page 91]

﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ [al-Qasas: 50] that "bighayri huda" (without guidance) is an emphasising circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida), not a restrictive one, since desire exists only without guidance.

The definiteness of "al-hawa" is the definiteness of genus (ta'rif al-jins).

The definiteness of "al-ma'wa" in the first and second occurrences is definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), that is, the refuge of him who transgressed, and the refuge of him who feared the standing before his Lord. This definiteness dispenses with mentioning what "refuge" is attributed to, and such usage is common in speech, as in the saying: "lower the gaze," meaning the gaze known from the context, that is, lower your gaze; and in the saying: "fill the ear," meaning your ear; and in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the heights are men﴾ [al-A'raf: 46], meaning upon the heights of the barrier. Therefore the estimated form of the sentence, according to the grammarians of Basra, is "a refuge for him" (al-ma'wa lahu), and according to the grammarians of Kufa, "his refuge" (ma'wahu). The Kufan grammarians call this "alif" and "lam" a substitute (iwad) for the attributed noun, which is a fine designation for its clarity and brevity, while the Basrans reject it. This is a slight disagreement, since the meaning is agreed upon.

Al-ma'wa is the name of a place, from "awa," meaning to return. What is meant by it is the abode and dwelling, because a person goes out to attend to his affairs and then returns to his dwelling.

And "maqam rabbihi" (the standing before his Lord) is a metaphor for majesty and awe. The original meaning of "maqam" is the place of standing, so its origin is the place of what is attributed to it. Then its use became common for the very thing it is attributed to, by way of metonymy (kinaya), glorifying the place in order to glorify its owner, like the words: janab, kanaf, and dhura (all meaning the protective side or presence). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But for whoever feared the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], and He said: ﴿That is for whoever fears My standing﴾ [Ibrahim: 14]. This is of the kind of metonymy in which a relation is sought to the thing metonymically referred to, for the fear of the standing of Allah means the fear of Allah, and by "relation" is meant what includes the connection to the object.

In His saying ﴿On the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ up to His saying ﴿Indeed, Paradise will be his refuge﴾ there is the embellishment of combining with division (muhassin al-jam' ma'a al-taqsim).

[Page 92]

The definiteness of "al-nafs" (the soul) in His saying ﴿and restrained the soul﴾ is like the definiteness in "al-ma'wa."

In the definiteness of "the companions of Hellfire" (ashab al-jahim) and "the companions of Paradise" (ashab al-jannah) by way of the relative clause, there is an indication that the two relative clauses are the two causes for entitlement to that refuge.

Therefore resurrection is expressed at the outset as "the quaking one" because it is its beginning, then as "the blast" (al-zajra), and finally as "the Great Catastrophe" (al-tammah al-kubra), because these two descriptions contain a meaning that encompasses the quaking and the terrors that follow it until each party settles in its abode.

And among the completeness of the appropriateness (munasaba) for reminding of the Day of Recompense is that it comes after the reminder of the creation of the earth and the favour of what He prepared from it for man as provision, indicating that this provision ends when the Day of Resurrection and Recompense arrives.

It is also possible to make His saying: ﴿So when the Great Catastrophe comes﴾ a consequence of His saying: ﴿It is but one blast﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 13] ﴿and at once they are on the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 14], for the Catastrophe is the Blast.

The basis of the consequence (manat al-tafri') is what follows it of detail in His saying: ﴿As for him who transgressed﴾ and so on, for it is not appropriate for a thing to be made a consequence of itself.

The particle (idha) denotes the future, so when it is followed by a past-tense verb, it is turned toward the future. The past tense is used after (idha) only to increase the confirmation of what (idha) conveys of the certainty of occurrence.

Al-majiy' (coming) here is a metaphor (majaz) for occurrence and taking place, because a thing fixed and deferred to a term resembles a person travelling toward a goal; when that deferred thing arrives at its appointed time, it is as if the traveller has reached the intended place.

Al-tammah (the Catastrophe) is the event or calamity that overwhelms (tamm), i.e., rises high and prevails, meaning it surpasses its like within its kind such that its equal is rare in its kind. It is derived from "tamma al-ma'" (the water overflowed) when it covers things. This description indicates severity and terror, for such a term is used only for dreadful matters. Then its dreadfulness is emphasised by describing it as "the Great" (al-kubra), and this is the clearest of expressions for depicting the terrors that accompany the event.

What is meant by "the Great Catastrophe" is the Resurrection, and it has been described in the Qur'an with many attributes, such as "the Deafening Blast" (al-sakhkha), "the Striking Calamity" (al-qari'a), "the Quaking" (al-raji'a), and it has been described as "the Great."

His saying: ﴿On the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the clause ﴿So when the Great Catastrophe comes﴾, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because what is added to the word "day" is one of the circumstances that the time of the arrival of the Catastrophe, which is the Day of Resurrection and the Day of Reckoning, includes. And man's remembering what he strove for means that his deeds in his record are presented to him, because "tadhakkur" (remembering) is the reflexive form (mutawi') of "dhakkara" (to cause to remember).

Remembering presupposes a prior forgetting, which is the effacement of what was known from the memory.

The meaning is: on the day he is reminded and so he remembers, that is, his deed is presented to him and he acknowledges it, for the purpose of remembering is nothing but its effect, which is the recompense. So remembering is used as a metonymy (kinaya) for recompense. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Read your record; sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾ [al-Isra': 14].

Tabriz al-jahim (the bringing forth of Hellfire) means its being displayed to its inhabitants. The verb in its doubled form (al-fi'l al-mudda'af) is used to convey the display of Hellfire, because it is a display for the purpose of terrifying.

Al-jahim is Jahannam. For this reason its verb is joined to the feminine ta' marbuta, because Jahannam is feminine in usage, or it is understood as "al-nar" (the Fire). Al-jahim is every great fire in a deep pit.

The verb "burrizat" is in the passive voice, because the identity of the one who brings it forth is not the purpose, since the admonition lies in informing of the occurrence of its being brought forth on that day.

As for His saying ﴿for whoever sees﴾, that is, for every seer, the verb "yara" (sees) is treated as intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lazim), because what is intended is "for whoever has sight," as in the saying of al-Buhturi:

"That the one who sees may see, and the one who hears, may listen."

The fa' in His saying ﴿As for him who transgressed﴾ is a link (rabita) for the response of (idha), because the clause "who transgressed" to its end is a nominal clause that contains no verb to which (idha) is attached, so there was no lexical connection between (idha) and its response. Therefore the fa' is brought in to link the response in the surface wording. As for meaning, it is known that (idha) is an adverb that is attached to the sense of stability that lies between the subject and the predicate.

(Amma) is a particle of detail and conditionality, because it carries the sense of "whatever may be the case."

Transgression (al-tughyan) has had its meaning mentioned just before, and what is meant here is that he transgressed against the command of Allah, as indicated by His saying: ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾.

The mention of transgression was placed before preferring the worldly life, because transgression is among the greatest causes of preferring the worldly life. Since it is the cause of it, it is mentioned right after it, observing the natural order.

Preference (al-iytar) is to prefer one thing over another in a state where it is not possible to combine the conditions of both.

The verb of preference is transitively extended to the object preferred by directly taking its object, and it is extended to the thing it is preferred over by the particle "ʿala" (over). Allah the Exalted said, relating: ﴿Indeed, Allah has preferred you over us﴾ [Yusuf: 91]. The mention of what is preferred over may be omitted when the mention of the preferred thing points to it, as when the preferred and the preferred-over are opposites, as here, due to the common contrast between the worldly life and the Hereafter.

The mention of the preferred may also be omitted, being satisfied with the mention of what is preferred over, when that is the more important, as in His saying: ﴿And they prefer [others] over themselves﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], since it is evident that what is meant is that they prefer "the poor."

[Page 90]

What is meant by "the worldly life" is its portions and benefits specific to it, that is, those that the portions of the Hereafter do not share with it. So the speech is with an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf), its estimated form being: "the bliss of the life."

It is understood from the verb of preference that with it there is a rejection of the bliss of the Hereafter. The preference for the worldly life returns to the satisfaction of the soul's desire, and both portions are known only through divine stipulation, just as shirk, the denial of the messengers, aggression against people, insolence, arrogance, and what follows from these of blameworthy states are known.

The essence of this preference is transgression against the command of Allah, for their leaders and those who direct them know that what the Messenger calls them to is the truth, but they hate following him out of arrogance, refusing to become followers of others, lest their dominion be lost. This meaning is further clarified by His saying after it: ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ and so on. From this it becomes clear that the basis of blame in preferring the worldly life is preferring it over the Hereafter. As for taking from the portions of the worldly life, which taking them does not forfeit the portions of the Hereafter, that is not blameworthy, and it is the station of many of the righteous servants of Allah, which Allah the Exalted relates about the righteous among the Children of Israel, in their saying to Qarun: ﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your portion of the world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77].

His saying ﴿who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ is the counterpart of His saying "who transgressed," because fear is the opposite of transgression. And His saying ﴿and restrained the soul from desire﴾ is the counterpart of His saying ﴿and preferred the worldly life﴾.

The restraining of the fearful person of his soul is used metaphorically (isti'ara) for refraining from taking what the soul loves of sins and desires. So the human soul is made like another person who calls him to evil deeds while he forbids him from this call. This resembles what is called "tajrid" (abstraction), as they say: "his soul told him such-and-such, so he disobeyed it," and it is said: "he forbade his heart." Among the finest of what has been said in this regard is the saying of 'Urwa ibn Udhayna:

"When I find for it whispers of consolation,
the heart interceded with the conscience, so it stilled it."

What is meant by "desire" (al-hawa) is what the soul desires. It is a verbal noun in the sense of the object, like "khalq" in the sense of "makhluq" (created thing). It is what the appetitive and irascible powers of the soul incline toward, of what opposes the truth and complete benefit. Desire has become common in reference to blameworthy inclinations, and for this reason it has been said regarding His saying:

The definiteness of "al-hawa" is the definiteness of genus (ta'rif al-jins).

This definiteness dispenses with mentioning what "refuge" is attributed to, and such usage is common in speech, as in the saying: "lower the gaze," meaning the gaze known from the context, that is, lower your gaze; and in the saying: "fill the ear," meaning your ear; and in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the heights are men﴾ [al-A'raf: 46], meaning upon the heights of the barrier. Then its dreadfulness is emphasised by describing it as "the Great" (al-kubra), and this is the clearest of expressions for depicting the terrors that accompany the event.

What is meant by "the Great Catastrophe" is the Resurrection, and it has been described in the Qur'an with many attributes, such as "the Deafening Blast" (al-sakhkha), "the Striking Calamity" (al-qari'a), "the Quaking" (al-raji'a), and it has been described as "the Great."

His saying: ﴿On the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the clause ﴿So when the Great Catastrophe comes﴾, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because what is added to the word "day" is one of the circumstances that the time of the arrival of the Catastrophe, which is the Day of Resurrection and the Day of Reckoning, includes. And man's remembering what he strove for means that his deeds in his record are presented to him, because "tadhakkur" (remembering) is the reflexive form (mutawi') of "dhakkara" (to cause to remember).

Remembering presupposes a prior forgetting, which is the effacement of what was known from the memory.

The meaning is: on the day he is reminded and so he remembers, that is, his deed is presented to him and he acknowledges it, for the purpose of remembering is nothing but its effect, which is the recompense. So remembering is used as a metonymy (kinaya) for recompense. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Read your record; sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾ [al-Isra': 14].

Tabriz al-jahim (the bringing forth of Hellfire) means its being displayed to its inhabitants. The verb in its doubled form (al-fi'l al-mudda'af) is used to convey the display of Hellfire, because it is a display for the purpose of terrifying.

Al-jahim is Jahannam. For this reason its verb is joined to the feminine ta' marbuta, because Jahannam is feminine in usage, or it is understood as "al-nar" (the Fire). Al-jahim is every great fire in a deep pit.

The verb "burrizat" is in the passive voice, because the identity of the one who brings it forth is not the purpose, since the admonition lies in informing of the occurrence of its being brought forth on that day.

As for His saying ﴿for whoever sees﴾, that is, for every seer, the verb "yara" (sees) is treated as intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lazim), because what is intended is "for whoever has sight," as in the saying of al-Buhturi:

"That the one who sees may see, and the one who hears, may listen."

The fa' in His saying ﴿As for him who transgressed﴾ is a link (rabita) for the response of (idha), because the clause "who transgressed" to its end is a nominal clause that contains no verb to which (idha) is attached, so there was no lexical connection between (idha) and its response. Therefore the fa' is brought in to link the response in the surface wording. As for meaning, it is known that (idha) is an adverb that is attached to the sense of stability that lies between the subject and the predicate.

(Amma) is a particle of detail and conditionality, because it carries the sense of "whatever may be the case."

Transgression (al-tughyan) has had its meaning mentioned just before, and what is meant here is that he transgressed against the command of Allah, as indicated by His saying: ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾.

The mention of transgression was placed before preferring the worldly life, because transgression is among the greatest causes of preferring the worldly life. Since it is the cause of it, it is mentioned right after it, observing the natural order.

Preference (al-iytar) is to prefer one thing over another in a state where it is not possible to combine the conditions of both.

The verb of preference is transitively extended to the object preferred by directly taking its object, and it is extended to the thing it is preferred over by the particle "ʿala" (over). Allah the Exalted said, relating: ﴿Indeed, Allah has preferred you over us﴾ [Yusuf: 91]. The mention of what is preferred over may be omitted when the mention of the preferred thing points to it, as when the preferred and the preferred-over are opposites, as here, due to the common contrast between the worldly life and the Hereafter.

The mention of the preferred may also be omitted, being satisfied with the mention of what is preferred over, when that is the more important, as in His saying: ﴿And they prefer [others] over themselves﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], since it is evident that what is meant is that they prefer "the poor."

[Page 90]

What is meant by "the worldly life" is its portions and benefits specific to it, that is, those that the portions of the Hereafter do not share with it. So the speech is with an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf), its estimated form being: "the bliss of the life."

It is understood from the verb of preference that with it there is a rejection of the bliss of the Hereafter. The preference for the worldly life returns to the satisfaction of the soul's desire, and both portions are known only through divine stipulation, just as shirk, the denial of the messengers, aggression against people, insolence, arrogance, and what follows from these of blameworthy states are known.

The essence of this preference is transgression against the command of Allah, for their leaders and those who direct them know that what the Messenger calls them to is the truth, but they hate following him out of arrogance, refusing to become followers of others, lest their dominion be lost. This meaning is further clarified by His saying after it: ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ and so on. From this it becomes clear that the basis of blame in preferring the worldly life is preferring it over the Hereafter. As for taking from the portions of the worldly life, which taking them does not forfeit the portions of the Hereafter, that is not blameworthy, and it is the station of many of the righteous servants of Allah, which Allah the Exalted relates about the righteous among the Children of Israel, in their saying to Qarun: ﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your portion of the world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77].

His saying ﴿who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ is the counterpart of His saying "who transgressed," because fear is the opposite of transgression. And His saying ﴿and restrained the soul from desire﴾ is the counterpart of His saying ﴿and preferred the worldly life﴾.

The restraining of the fearful person of his soul is used metaphorically (isti'ara) for refraining from taking what the soul loves of sins and desires. So the human soul is made like another person who calls him to evil deeds while he forbids him from this call. This resembles what is called "tajrid" (abstraction), as they say: "his soul told him such-and-such, so he disobeyed it," and it is said: "he forbade his heart." Among the finest of what has been said in this regard is the saying of 'Urwa ibn Udhayna:

"When I find for it whispers of consolation,
the heart interceded with the conscience, so it stilled it."

What is meant by "desire" (al-hawa) is what the soul desires. It is a verbal noun in the sense of the object, like "khalq" in the sense of "makhluq" (created thing). It is what the appetitive and irascible powers of the soul incline toward, of what opposes the truth and complete benefit. Desire has become common in reference to blameworthy inclinations, and for this reason it has been said regarding His saying:

[Page 91]

﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ [al-Qasas: 50] that "bighayri huda" (without guidance) is an emphasising circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida), not a restrictive one, since desire exists only without guidance.

The definiteness of "al-hawa" is the definiteness of genus (ta'rif al-jins).

The definiteness of "al-ma'wa" in the first and second occurrences is definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), that is, the refuge of him who transgressed, and the refuge of him who feared the standing before his Lord. This definiteness dispenses with mentioning what "refuge" is attributed to, and such usage is common in speech, as in the saying: "lower the gaze," meaning the gaze known from the context, that is, lower your gaze; and in the saying: "fill the ear," meaning your ear; and in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the heights are men﴾ [al-A'raf: 46], meaning upon the heights of the barrier. Therefore the estimated form of the sentence, according to the grammarians of Basra, is "a refuge for him" (al-ma'wa lahu), and according to the grammarians of Kufa, "his refuge" (ma'wahu). The Kufan grammarians call this "alif" and "lam" a substitute (iwad) for the attributed noun, which is a fine designation for its clarity and brevity, while the Basrans reject it. This is a slight disagreement, since the meaning is agreed upon.

Al-ma'wa is the name of a place, from "awa," meaning to return. What is meant by it is the abode and dwelling, because a person goes out to attend to his affairs and then returns to his dwelling.

And "maqam rabbihi" (the standing before his Lord) is a metaphor for majesty and awe. The original meaning of "maqam" is the place of standing, so its origin is the place of what is attributed to it. Then its use became common for the very thing it is attributed to, by way of metonymy (kinaya), glorifying the place in order to glorify its owner, like the words: janab, kanaf, and dhura (all meaning the protective side or presence). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But for whoever feared the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], and He said: ﴿That is for whoever fears My standing﴾ [Ibrahim: 14]. This is of the kind of metonymy in which a relation is sought to the thing metonymically referred to, for the fear of the standing of Allah means the fear of Allah, and by "relation" is meant what includes the connection to the object.

In His saying ﴿On the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ up to His saying ﴿Indeed, Paradise will be his refuge﴾ there is the embellishment of combining with division (muhassin al-jam' ma'a al-taqsim).

As for His saying ﴿for whoever sees﴾, that is, for every seer, the verb "yara" (sees) is treated as intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lazim), because what is intended is "for whoever has sight," as in the saying of al-Buhturi:

"That the one who sees may see, and the one who hears, may listen."

The fa' in His saying ﴿As for him who transgressed﴾ is a link (rabita) for the response of (idha), because the clause "who transgressed" to its end is a nominal clause that contains no verb to which (idha) is attached, so there was no lexical connection between (idha) and its response. Therefore the fa' is brought in to link the response in the surface wording. As for meaning, it is known that (idha) is an adverb that is attached to the sense of stability that lies between the subject and the predicate.

(Amma) is a particle of detail and conditionality, because it carries the sense of "whatever may be the case."

Transgression (al-tughyan) has had its meaning mentioned just before, and what is meant here is that he transgressed against the command of Allah, as indicated by His saying: ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾.

The mention of transgression was placed before preferring the worldly life, because transgression is among the greatest causes of preferring the worldly life. Since it is the cause of it, it is mentioned right after it, observing the natural order.

Preference (al-iytar) is to prefer one thing over another in a state where it is not possible to combine the conditions of both.

The verb of preference is transitively extended to the object preferred by directly taking its object, and it is extended to the thing it is preferred over by the particle "ʿala" (over). Allah the Exalted said, relating: ﴿Indeed, Allah has preferred you over us﴾ [Yusuf: 91]. The mention of what is preferred over may be omitted when the mention of the preferred thing points to it, as when the preferred and the preferred-over are opposites, as here, due to the common contrast between the worldly life and the Hereafter.

The mention of the preferred may also be omitted, being satisfied with the mention of what is preferred over, when that is the more important, as in His saying: ﴿And they prefer [others] over themselves﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], since it is evident that what is meant is that they prefer "the poor."

[Page 90]

What is meant by "the worldly life" is its portions and benefits specific to it, that is, those that the portions of the Hereafter do not share with it. So the speech is with an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf), its estimated form being: "the bliss of the life."

It is understood from the verb of preference that with it there is a rejection of the bliss of the Hereafter. The preference for the worldly life returns to the satisfaction of the soul's desire, and both portions are known only through divine stipulation, just as shirk, the denial of the messengers, aggression against people, insolence, arrogance, and what follows from these of blameworthy states are known.

The essence of this preference is transgression against the command of Allah, for their leaders and those who direct them know that what the Messenger calls them to is the truth, but they hate following him out of arrogance, refusing to become followers of others, lest their dominion be lost. This meaning is further clarified by His saying after it: ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ and so on. From this it becomes clear that the basis of blame in preferring the worldly life is preferring it over the Hereafter. As for taking from the portions of the worldly life, which taking them does not forfeit the portions of the Hereafter, that is not blameworthy, and it is the station of many of the righteous servants of Allah, which Allah the Exalted relates about the righteous among the Children of Israel, in their saying to Qarun: ﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your portion of the world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77].

His saying ﴿who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ is the counterpart of His saying "who transgressed," because fear is the opposite of transgression. And His saying ﴿and restrained the soul from desire﴾ is the counterpart of His saying ﴿and preferred the worldly life﴾.

The restraining of the fearful person of his soul is used metaphorically (isti'ara) for refraining from taking what the soul loves of sins and desires. So the human soul is made like another person who calls him to evil deeds while he forbids him from this call. This resembles what is called "tajrid" (abstraction), as they say: "his soul told him such-and-such, so he disobeyed it," and it is said: "he forbade his heart." Among the finest of what has been said in this regard is the saying of 'Urwa ibn Udhayna:

"When I find for it whispers of consolation,
the heart interceded with the conscience, so it stilled it."

What is meant by "desire" (al-hawa) is what the soul desires. It is a verbal noun in the sense of the object, like "khalq" in the sense of "makhluq" (created thing). It is what the appetitive and irascible powers of the soul incline toward, of what opposes the truth and complete benefit. Desire has become common in reference to blameworthy inclinations, and for this reason it has been said regarding His saying:

[Page 91]

﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ [al-Qasas: 50] that "bighayri huda" (without guidance) is an emphasising circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida), not a restrictive one, since desire exists only without guidance.

The definiteness of "al-hawa" is the definiteness of genus (ta'rif al-jins).

The definiteness of "al-ma'wa" in the first and second occurrences is definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), that is, the refuge of him who transgressed, and the refuge of him who feared the standing before his Lord. This definiteness dispenses with mentioning what "refuge" is attributed to, and such usage is common in speech, as in the saying: "lower the gaze," meaning the gaze known from the context, that is, lower your gaze; and in the saying: "fill the ear," meaning your ear; and in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the heights are men﴾ [al-A'raf: 46], meaning upon the heights of the barrier. Therefore the estimated form of the sentence, according to the grammarians of Basra, is "a refuge for him" (al-ma'wa lahu), and according to the grammarians of Kufa, "his refuge" (ma'wahu). The Kufan grammarians call this "alif" and "lam" a substitute (iwad) for the attributed noun, which is a fine designation for its clarity and brevity, while the Basrans reject it. This is a slight disagreement, since the meaning is agreed upon.

Al-ma'wa is the name of a place, from "awa," meaning to return. What is meant by it is the abode and dwelling, because a person goes out to attend to his affairs and then returns to his dwelling.

And "maqam rabbihi" (the standing before his Lord) is a metaphor for majesty and awe. The original meaning of "maqam" is the place of standing, so its origin is the place of what is attributed to it. Then its use became common for the very thing it is attributed to, by way of metonymy (kinaya), glorifying the place in order to glorify its owner, like the words: janab, kanaf, and dhura (all meaning the protective side or presence). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But for whoever feared the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], and He said: ﴿That is for whoever fears My standing﴾ [Ibrahim: 14]. This is of the kind of metonymy in which a relation is sought to the thing metonymically referred to, for the fear of the standing of Allah means the fear of Allah, and by "relation" is meant what includes the connection to the object.

In His saying ﴿On the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ up to His saying ﴿Indeed, Paradise will be his refuge﴾ there is the embellishment of combining with division (muhassin al-jam' ma'a al-taqsim).

[Page 92]

The definiteness of "al-nafs" (the soul) in His saying ﴿and restrained the soul﴾ is like the definiteness in "al-ma'wa."

In the definiteness of "the companions of Hellfire" (ashab al-jahim) and "the companions of Paradise" (ashab al-jannah) by way of the relative clause, there is an indication that the two relative clauses are the two causes for entitlement to that refuge.

[Page 89]

﴿So when the Great Catastrophe comes﴾ ﴿On the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ ﴿And Hellfire is brought forth for whoever sees﴾ ﴿As for him who transgressed﴾ ﴿And preferred the worldly life﴾ ﴿Indeed, Hellfire will be his refuge﴾ ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire﴾ ﴿Indeed, Paradise will be his refuge﴾.

It is possible that this is a consequence (tafri') of the argument contained in His saying: ﴿Are you more difficult to create or is the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27] and what follows it. For the establishment of resurrection necessitates recompense, since recompense is its wisdom. When recompense is necessitated, it is incumbent upon the rational person to act for the reward of the good (al-husna), to avoid what leads to wretchedness, to care for the everlasting life and prefer it, and not to be indifferent to a transient bliss so as to become entangled in pursuing it. Therefore, after the proof for the establishment of resurrection, there follows a reminder of the two recompenses and guidance toward the two paths (al-najdayn).

Since a general warning had already been given before the argument, in His saying: ﴿On the day when the quaking one quakes﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 6] and what follows, just as the thesis (al-matlub) is mentioned before the syllogism (qiyas) in dialectic (jadal), after the argument there came a detailed explanation of that warning, combined with good tidings for whoever adorns himself with its opposite. Therefore resurrection is expressed at the outset as "the quaking one" because it is its beginning, then as "the blast" (al-zajra), and finally as "the Great Catastrophe" (al-tammah al-kubra), because these two descriptions contain a meaning that encompasses the quaking and the terrors that follow it until each party settles in its abode.

And among the completeness of the appropriateness (munasaba) for reminding of the Day of Recompense is that it comes after the reminder of the creation of the earth and the favour of what He prepared from it for man as provision, indicating that this provision ends when the Day of Resurrection and Recompense arrives.

It is also possible to make His saying: ﴿So when the Great Catastrophe comes﴾ a consequence of His saying: ﴿It is but one blast﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 13] ﴿and at once they are on the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 14], for the Catastrophe is the Blast.

The basis of the consequence (manat al-tafri') is what follows it of detail in His saying: ﴿As for him who transgressed﴾ and so on, for it is not appropriate for a thing to be made a consequence of itself.

The particle (idha) denotes the future, so when it is followed by a past-tense verb, it is turned toward the future. The past tense is used after (idha) only to increase the confirmation of what (idha) conveys of the certainty of occurrence.

Al-majiy' (coming) here is a metaphor (majaz) for occurrence and taking place, because a thing fixed and deferred to a term resembles a person travelling toward a goal; when that deferred thing arrives at its appointed time, it is as if the traveller has reached the intended place.

Al-tammah (the Catastrophe) is the event or calamity that overwhelms (tamm), i.e., rises high and prevails, meaning it surpasses its like within its kind such that its equal is rare in its kind. It is derived from "tamma al-ma'" (the water overflowed) when it covers things. This description indicates severity and terror, for such a term is used only for dreadful matters. Then its dreadfulness is emphasised by describing it as "the Great" (al-kubra), and this is the clearest of expressions for depicting the terrors that accompany the event.

What is meant by "the Great Catastrophe" is the Resurrection, and it has been described in the Qur'an with many attributes, such as "the Deafening Blast" (al-sakhkha), "the Striking Calamity" (al-qari'a), "the Quaking" (al-raji'a), and it has been described as "the Great."

His saying: ﴿On the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the clause ﴿So when the Great Catastrophe comes﴾, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because what is added to the word "day" is one of the circumstances that the time of the arrival of the Catastrophe, which is the Day of Resurrection and the Day of Reckoning, includes. And man's remembering what he strove for means that his deeds in his record are presented to him, because "tadhakkur" (remembering) is the reflexive form (mutawi') of "dhakkara" (to cause to remember).

Remembering presupposes a prior forgetting, which is the effacement of what was known from the memory.

The meaning is: on the day he is reminded and so he remembers, that is, his deed is presented to him and he acknowledges it, for the purpose of remembering is nothing but its effect, which is the recompense. So remembering is used as a metonymy (kinaya) for recompense. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Read your record; sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾ [al-Isra': 14].

(﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its appointed time?﴾ ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ ﴿Its final knowledge rests with your Lord.﴾ ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾)

.

It is a explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), arising from the fact that the polytheists used to ask about the time when the Hour, with which the Prophet ﷺ threatened them, would arrive, as God related about them more than once in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48].

Their question was mockery and belittlement, because they had fixed their hearts on the impossibility of the Hour occurring. Perhaps they sought to hasten its occurrence, and they led themselves and their followers to imagine that the delay in its occurrence was a sign of its being hopeless, because they imagined that if they did this with the Messenger ﷺ, and he were truthful, the anger of God who sent him - glorified is He - would be stirred, so He would hasten to show them the punishment. They imagined the affairs of the Creator to be like the affairs of people, when one of them becomes angry he hastens to take revenge out of recklessness and rage. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If God were to take them to account for what they earned, He would have hastened punishment for them. But for them there is an appointed time from which they will find no refuge other than Him.﴾ [al-Kahf: 58].

Therefore, when the proof of the possibility of resurrection had been established through presenting evidence and striking parables, and an allusion was made to the punishment of those who belittled it in His saying: ﴿So when the great calamity comes﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 34], this became an occasion for their asking: "Is there a known time for the coming of this great calamity?" The situation therefore required this explanatory resumptive sentence, to fulfil the requirement of the context and to answer what preceded in the speech.

The pronoun in (يَسْألُونَ) refers to the polytheists, the owners of the trembling hearts, and those who said ﴿Shall we indeed be returned to our former state?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 10].

[Page 95]
The verb of asking is expressed in the present tense to indicate the renewal and recurrence of this question.

"The Hour" (al-sa'ah) is the great calamity (al-ṭammah). The mention of "the Hour" is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun, for the purpose of making the sentence independent in its meaning, along with variety in expressing it through these two names: (al-ṭammah) and (al-sā'ah).

And (﴿أيّانَ مُرْساها﴾), "when is its appointed time," is a sentence explaining the question.

And (أيّانَ) is a noun used to ask about specifying the time.

The interrogation is used for disapproval (istib'ad) as a metonymy, and it is also a metonymy for impossibility. (مُرْساها) is a noun of place/time (maṣdar mimi) from the verb (أرْسى), and iršā' (anchoring) is making a ship stop at the shore for the purpose of disembarking from it. The term "anchoring" is used metaphorically for occurrence and taking place, likening the hidden event's occurrence to a ship sailing the sea, whose arrival is not known except when it anchors. Accordingly, (أيّانَ) is a supporting element (tarshih) for the metaphor, and a parallel to this appeared in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying: ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ stands in the position of an answer to their question about the Hour, in view of what appears from the state of their question about the Hour, namely their desire to specify its time while diverting attention from their intention of mockery. This answer is therefore an expression of the speech contrary to the requirement of the apparent meaning. It is a way of addressing the questioner with something other than what he seeks, as an alert to him that it is better for him to be concerned with something else, which is the content of His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾ This is what is called the wise method (al-uslub al-hakim), and a parallel to it is what is related in the Sahih that "a man asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Hour, and he said to him: 'What have you prepared for it?'" That is: it would have been better for you to direct your care to increasing good deeds, preparing for the day of the Hour.

Although the address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, the intended meaning is that it reaches the ears of the polytheists. Therefore it is treated as an answer to their speech, and this is what requires separating the sentence from the one before it, as is the case with answer and question.

The (ما) in His saying (فِيمَ) is an interrogative noun meaning "what thing?", used for expressing wonder at the questioners' question about it, and then rebuking them. (فِي) is for figurative enclosure, as if the polytheists, in their insistence in asking about the time of the Hour, had made the Prophet ﷺ encompassed by mention of the time of the Hour, that is, engaged with it in the manner of one knowledgeable with what is known. This is indicated by the particle of enclosure in the manner of metaphor in the particle.

The alif of (ما) is omitted because it comes after a preposition, as in ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1]. (فِيمَ) is a predicate placed first, and (أنْتَ) is the subject, and (مِن ذِكْراها) is either related to the stability contained in the predicate, or it is a circumstantial element (ḥāl) of the subject.

(مِن) is either explaining the ambiguity in the interrogative (ما), meaning: "in a thing which is its mention," that is, in a thing which is your mentioning it; that is, you are not occupied with a thing which is the reminder of the Hour. Or it is a descriptor of the subject, in which case it is connective (ittiṣāliyyah), a kind of initial (ibtida'iyyah) whose initiation is figurative, meaning: you are not in a thing that connects with the mention of the Hour and hovers around it, that is, you are not in a thing which is the mention of the time of the Hour. And according to the second: you are not in connection with the mention of the Hour, that is, there is no association between you and specifying its time.

Placing (فِيمَ) before the subject is for the purpose of emphasizing it, to convey that the content of the predicate is the basis of the denial, unlike if it were said: "Are you in a thing of its mention?" The reminder (al-dhikrā) is the verbal noun of remembrance, and what is meant here is verbal mention.

The clause ﴿Its final knowledge rests with your Lord﴾ serves as the reason for the denial that His saying ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ required, and therefore it is separated. In the speech there is an omitted modifier, and the meaning is: "The knowledge of its final point rests with your Lord."

Placing the prepositional phrase before the subject in His saying ﴿Its final knowledge rests with your Lord﴾ is to convey restriction (qaṣr), that is, not with you. This is a restriction of an attribute to a qualified subject.

Al-muntahā: its origin is the place where a journey ends, then it was applied to the destination, because arrival is necessarily connected to ending. God said: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾ [al-Najm: 42]. Then it was extended and applied to knowledge, that is, none knows it except God. So His saying (﴿مُنْتَهاها﴾) in meaning is with an omitted modifier, that is, the knowledge of the time of its occurrence, as indicated by His saying (﴿أيّانَ مُرْساها﴾).

It is also possible that (مُنْتَهاها) means the arrival of its news, as one says: "I brought to so-and-so the event of such-and-such," and "the news of such-and-such reached me."

Their question was mockery and belittlement, because they had fixed their hearts on the impossibility of the Hour occurring. Perhaps they sought to hasten its occurrence, and they led themselves and their followers to imagine that the delay in its occurrence was a sign of its being hopeless, because they imagined that if they did this with the Messenger ﷺ, and he were truthful, the anger of God who sent him - glorified is He - would be stirred, so He would hasten to show them the punishment. They imagined the affairs of the Creator to be like the affairs of people, when one of them becomes angry he hastens to take revenge out of recklessness and rage. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If God were to take them to account for what they earned, He would have hastened punishment for them. But for them there is an appointed time from which they will find no refuge other than Him.﴾ [al-Kahf: 58].

The verb of asking is expressed in the present tense to indicate the renewal and recurrence of this question.

"The Hour" (al-sa'ah) is the great calamity (al-ṭammah). The mention of "the Hour" is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun, for the purpose of making the sentence independent in its meaning, along with variety in expressing it through these two names: (al-ṭammah) and (al-sā'ah).

And (﴿أيّانَ مُرْساها﴾), "when is its appointed time," is a sentence explaining the question.

And (أيّانَ) is a noun used to ask about specifying the time.

The interrogation is used for disapproval (istib'ad) as a metonymy, and it is also a metonymy for impossibility. (مُرْساها) is a noun of place/time (maṣdar mimi) from the verb (أرْسى), and iršā' (anchoring) is making a ship stop at the shore for the purpose of disembarking from it. The term "anchoring" is used metaphorically for occurrence and taking place, likening the hidden event's occurrence to a ship sailing the sea, whose arrival is not known except when it anchors. Accordingly, (أيّانَ) is a supporting element (tarshih) for the metaphor, and a parallel to this appeared in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying: ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ stands in the position of an answer to their question about the Hour, in view of what appears from the state of their question about the Hour, namely their desire to specify its time while diverting attention from their intention of mockery. This answer is therefore an expression of the speech contrary to the requirement of the apparent meaning. It is a way of addressing the questioner with something other than what he seeks, as an alert to him that it is better for him to be concerned with something else, which is the content of His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾ This is what is called the wise method (al-uslub al-hakim), and a parallel to it is what is related in the Sahih that "a man asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Hour, and he said to him: 'What have you prepared for it?'" That is: it would have been better for you to direct your care to increasing good deeds, preparing for the day of the Hour.

Although the address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, the intended meaning is that it reaches the ears of the polytheists. Therefore it is treated as an answer to their speech, and this is what requires separating the sentence from the one before it, as is the case with answer and question.

The (ما) in His saying (فِيمَ) is an interrogative noun meaning "what thing?", used for expressing wonder at the questioners' question about it, and then rebuking them. (فِي) is for figurative enclosure, as if the polytheists, in their insistence in asking about the time of the Hour, had made the Prophet ﷺ encompassed by mention of the time of the Hour, that is, engaged with it in the manner of one knowledgeable with what is known. This is indicated by the particle of enclosure in the manner of metaphor in the particle.

The alif of (ما) is omitted because it comes after a preposition, as in ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1]. (فِيمَ) is a predicate placed first, and (أنْتَ) is the subject, and (مِن ذِكْراها) is either related to the stability contained in the predicate, or it is a circumstantial element (ḥāl) of the subject.

(مِن) is either explaining the ambiguity in the interrogative (ما), meaning: "in a thing which is its mention," that is, in a thing which is your mentioning it; that is, you are not occupied with a thing which is the reminder of the Hour. Or it is a descriptor of the subject, in which case it is connective (ittiṣāliyyah), a kind of initial (ibtida'iyyah) whose initiation is figurative, meaning: you are not in a thing that connects with the mention of the Hour and hovers around it, that is, you are not in a thing which is the mention of the time of the Hour. And according to the second: you are not in connection with the mention of the Hour, that is, there is no association between you and specifying its time.

Placing (فِيمَ) before the subject is for the purpose of emphasizing it, to convey that the content of the predicate is the basis of the denial, unlike if it were said: "Are you in a thing of its mention?" The reminder (al-dhikrā) is the verbal noun of remembrance, and what is meant here is verbal mention.

The clause ﴿Its final knowledge rests with your Lord﴾ serves as the reason for the denial that His saying ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ required, and therefore it is separated. In the speech there is an omitted modifier, and the meaning is: "The knowledge of its final point rests with your Lord."

This answer is therefore an expression of the speech contrary to the requirement of the apparent meaning. It is a way of addressing the questioner with something other than what he seeks, as an alert to him that it is better for him to be concerned with something else, which is the content of His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾ This is what is called the wise method (al-uslub al-hakim), and a parallel to it is what is related in the Sahih that "a man asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Hour, and he said to him: 'What have you prepared for it?'" That is: it would have been better for you to direct your care to increasing good deeds, preparing for the day of the Hour.

Although the address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, the intended meaning is that it reaches the ears of the polytheists. Therefore it is treated as an answer to their speech, and this is what requires separating the sentence from the one before it, as is the case with answer and question.

The (ما) in His saying (فِيمَ) is an interrogative noun meaning "what thing?", used for expressing wonder at the questioners' question about it, and then rebuking them. (فِي) is for figurative enclosure, as if the polytheists, in their insistence in asking about the time of the Hour, had made the Prophet ﷺ encompassed by mention of the time of the Hour, that is, engaged with it in the manner of one knowledgeable with what is known. This is indicated by the particle of enclosure in the manner of metaphor in the particle.

The alif of (ما) is omitted because it comes after a preposition, as in ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1]. (فِيمَ) is a predicate placed first, and (أنْتَ) is the subject, and (مِن ذِكْراها) is either related to the stability contained in the predicate, or it is a circumstantial element (ḥāl) of the subject.

(مِن) is either explaining the ambiguity in the interrogative (ما), meaning: "in a thing which is its mention," that is, in a thing which is your mentioning it; that is, you are not occupied with a thing which is the reminder of the Hour. Or it is a descriptor of the subject, in which case it is connective (ittiṣāliyyah), a kind of initial (ibtida'iyyah) whose initiation is figurative, meaning: you are not in a thing that connects with the mention of the Hour and hovers around it, that is, you are not in a thing which is the mention of the time of the Hour. And according to the second: you are not in connection with the mention of the Hour, that is, there is no association between you and specifying its time.

Placing (فِيمَ) before the subject is for the purpose of emphasizing it, to convey that the content of the predicate is the basis of the denial, unlike if it were said: "Are you in a thing of its mention?" The reminder (al-dhikrā) is the verbal noun of remembrance, and what is meant here is verbal mention.

The clause ﴿Its final knowledge rests with your Lord﴾ serves as the reason for the denial that His saying ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾ required, and therefore it is separated. In the speech there is an omitted modifier, and the meaning is: "The knowledge of its final point rests with your Lord."

Placing the prepositional phrase before the subject in His saying ﴿Its final knowledge rests with your Lord﴾ is to convey restriction (qaṣr), that is, not with you. This is a restriction of an attribute to a qualified subject.

Al-muntahā: its origin is the place where a journey ends, then it was applied to the destination, because arrival is necessarily connected to ending. God said: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾ [al-Najm: 42]. Then it was extended and applied to knowledge, that is, none knows it except God. So His saying (﴿مُنْتَهاها﴾) in meaning is with an omitted modifier, that is, the knowledge of the time of its occurrence, as indicated by His saying (﴿أيّانَ مُرْساها﴾).

It is also possible that (مُنْتَهاها) means the arrival of its news, as one says: "I brought to so-and-so the event of such-and-such," and "the news of such-and-such reached me."

[Page 96]
His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ is an explanatory resumptive sentence arising from the clause ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it? Its final knowledge rests with your Lord.﴾ The listener may ask about the reason for the Prophet ﷺ mentioning it frequently and that it is near, so he is answered that the Prophet's ﷺ share is warning against its sudden arrival, and his share is not informing about specifying its time. Moreover, the polytheists took the Qur'an's turning away from specifying its time as an argument for them against its possibility, because in their ignorance of realities they supposed that it is part of the Prophet's ﷺ role to know the unseen. For this reason the Qur'an repeatedly absolved the Prophet ﷺ of that, as in His saying: ﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of God, nor do I know the unseen﴾ [al-An'am: 50].

(إنَّما) conveys restriction of the addressee to the attribute of warning, that is, specifying him with the state of warning. It is a restriction of a qualified subject to an attribute, so it is a relative restriction (qaṣr idafi), that is, in relation to what they believed about him, as indicated by their persistent insistence in the question that he knows the unseen.

His saying: ﴿مُنْذِرُ مَن يَخْشاها﴾ is read by the majority with (مُنْذِرُ) construed as a genitive construction with (مَن يَخْشاها). Abu Ja'far read it with tanwin on (مُنْذِرُ), with (مَن يَخْشاها) as its object.

In the construct with (مُنْذِرُ) before (مَن يَخْشاها), or in its being in the accusative governed by it, there is an elliptical brevity (ījāz ḥadhf), whose estimate is: "warner of it, so the one who fears it is warned." Its indicator is contextual, due to the knowledge widely transmitted from the Qur'an that the Prophet ﷺ used to warn all people, not specifying one group over others. The verses of the call in the Qur'an and the stations of the Prophet's ﷺ call were only general. And no one is known as one who fears the Hour until after the believer has believed. If someone were known by name to never believe, the call would not have been directed to him. So it is established that the meaning is: he benefits from the warning only one who fears the Hour, while anyone other than him, the call passes by his hearing and he pays it no heed. Thus the mention of "those who fear it" serves to honour the believers, proclaim their distinction, and belittle those who remained in disbelief. God said: ﴿And you cannot make those in graves hear. You are only a warner﴾ [Fatir: 22].

On this principle it is understood why this address with faith was directed to people whom God knew would not believe, and reality revealed that they died without believing, such as the chiefs of Quraysh, the companions of the well at Badr, like Abu Jahl and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. And why the address calling for piety was directed to those whom God knew would not be pious, like the ruffians (du'ṣār) of the Arabs who embraced Islam but did not give up aggression and immoralities, and like the apostates who did not disbelieve among them but insisted on withholding zakat, and Abu Bakr - may God be pleased with him - fought them. Whoever died among them in that state is among those who did not fear God, because what is in God's knowledge is not reached by people's knowledge, and its final outcome does not become apparent except after death. This is the well-known question among our theologians (al-mutakallimun), called the question of al-muwafāh (the matter of final outcome).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 79, verse 46:

﴿As if, on the day they see it, they had not remained but for an evening or its morning.﴾

This is a response to what is implied by His words: ﴿They ask you about the Hour, "When will it take place?"﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 42]. Judging by the outward state of the question, it seeks knowledge of when the Hour will come, and expresses impatience at its delay, which they cite as a way of denying that it will occur. They were answered in the manner of the wise method of address (al-uslub al-hakim, a rhetorical approach that answers a question in a way that goes beyond its literal form), meaning: even if its arrival is long delayed, it will certainly happen, and on the day it happens they will feel as though they had waited only a part of a single day.

"Al-'Ashiyya" (the evening) is used to express a brief span within a long period, by way of comparison. This is derived from "ka'anna" (as if), so the comparison is between their state and the state of one who remained only an evening. The purpose of this comparison is to bring the meaning closer to what is familiar.

As for His words, ﴿or its morning﴾, it offers a choice within the comparison, in the same way as His words: ﴿or like a downpour from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19] in Surat al-Baqarah. This conjunction adds to the shortening of the span, because the portion of the morning (duha) is shorter than the portion of the evening.

The annexation of "duha" (morning) to the pronoun of "'ashiyya" follows a common Arabic usage in their speech. Al-Farra' said: "Al-duha was annexed to al-'ashiyya, which is the day in which, according to the custom of the Arabs, they say: 'I will come to you in the morning (al-ghadah) or its evening, and I will come to you in the evening or its morning.'" One of the Banu 'Uqayl recited to me:

"We attacked 'Amir in her abode, with swift horses whose two ends of the day were in opposition,
in the evening of the crescent or its last part."

He intended "the evening of the crescent or the evening of the last part of the evening," and this is stronger than: "I will come to you in the morning or its evening." (End of quotation.)

The justification for the annexation is that the morning precedes the evening, since an evening does not occur except after the passing of a morning. Thus the morning of that day is identified by its annexation to the evening of that day, because the evening is closer to people's knowledge: they are in the evening after having been in the morning. So the evening is nearer and the morning is earlier.

In this annexation there is also a consideration of the verse endings (fawasil), which end in the open letter ha' (ها), from "ayyana murساها" (when will it take place).

With the conclusion of this surah, the long surahs of the Mufassal (the final section of the Qur'an) are complete, the first of which is Surat al-Hujurat.

[Page 101]
In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful
Surat 'Abasa

This surah is named in the mushafs, in books of tafsir, and in books of Sunnah as "Surat 'Abasa."

In Ahkam al-Qur'an, Ibn al-'Arabi titled it "Surat Ibn Umm Maktum." I have not seen this from anyone else. Al-Khafaji said: it is called "Surat al-Sakhkha." Al-'Ayni, in his commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari, said: it is called "Surat al-Safara," and it is called "Surat al-A'mā" (the Blind Man's Surah). All of these names are taken from words that occur in it and do not occur in other surahs, or from the companion who is the subject of the story that was the occasion of its revelation.

Al-Suyuti, author of al-Itqan, did not mention it among the surahs that have more than one name, namely 'Abasa.

It is Meccan by consensus.

Al-'Ara'ida... [in al-'Arida] Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The scholars have not verified the determination of which revelations were in Mecca and which in Medina, in general, and the time of Ibn Umm Maktum's conversion to Islam cannot be verified." (End of quotation.) This contradicts the consensus of the people of tafsir that it is Meccan, so there is no substance to Ibn al-'Arabi's statement.

It is counted as the twenty-fourth surah in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat al-Najm and before Surat al-Qadr.

Its number of verses, according to the counters from the people of Medina, the people of Mecca, and the people of Kufa, is forty-two. According to the people of Basra it is forty-one, and according to the people of Syria it is forty.

It is the first of the surahs of the middle of the Mufassal.

The reason for its revelation will come at His words: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ [Abasa: 1].

* * *

[Page 102]
The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taught the balancing between degrees of benefits (masalih), and the obligation to investigate their hidden aspects, so that giving attention to the important among them at first glance does not cause him to miss another matter that is equal in importance or greater. For this reason, the scholars of usul al-fiqh (the foundations of jurisprudence) say: the mujtahid (qualified jurist) must search for a counter-indication to the evidence that has appeared to him.

The surah points to the difference in state between the polytheists who turn away from the guidance of Islam and the Muslims who are eager to pursue its teachings.

This is paired with a reminder of the honouring of the believers and the elevation of their rank with Allah, the Exalted.

It also praises the Qur'an and teaches it to whoever desires its knowledge.

The discussion moves from this to describing the severity of disbelief among the chieftains of Quraysh, through their obstinate rejection of the call, which occupied the Prophet (ﷺ) so that he did not turn to the desire of Ibn Umm Maktum.

It argues for the proof of resurrection, which is among the things they were called to when Ibn Umm Maktum was present. This was among the greatest matters the Qur'an was concerned with, since the denial of resurrection is the fundamental root of the polytheists' determination to turn away from the Qur'an's call, supposing that it calls to the impossible. So they were argued against by the creation of man, and then by the bringing forth of plants and trees from dead earth.

The argument is followed by a warning of the coming of the Hour, a caution about its terrors, and what follows it: the reward of the righteous and the punishment of the deniers.

It also reminds them of Allah's blessings upon the deniers, so that perhaps they will be thankful to Him.

It highlights the weak among the believers, the elevation of their status, the goodness that comes from their souls and their fear (of Allah), and that they are greater before Allah than the wealthy who have lost purity of soul, and that the latter deserve contempt and blame, and are people of disbelief and wickedness.
